verses.134:4: For the Lord chose Jacob for Himself, Israel as His special possession.
verses.134:5: For I know that the Lord is great, and our Lord is above all the gods.
verses.134:6: All that He willed, the Lord did in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in the depths.
verses.134:7: Bringing up clouds from the end of the earth, He made flashes of lightning for rain, He who brings out winds from His storehouses,
verses.134:8: who struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man to beast.
verses.134:9: He sent out signs and wonders in your midst, Egypt, against Pharaoh and against all his servants.
verses.134:10: He struck many nations and killed mighty kings:
verses.134:11: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan;
verses.134:12: and He gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel His servant.
verses.134:13: Lord, Your name is forever; Lord, Your remembrance is for generation after generation.
verses.134:14: The Lord has compassion on His people, and He will be comforted over His servants.
verses.134:15: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands.
verses.134:16: They have a mouth and do not speak; they have eyes and will not see.
verses.134:17: They have ears and will not listen, for there is not even breath in their mouth.
verses.134:18: May all who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.
verses.134:19: House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord.
verses.134:20: House of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.
verses.134:21: Blessed be the Lord from Zion, who inhabits Jerusalem.
verses.135:1: Hallelujah. Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:2: Give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:3: Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:4: to Him who alone does great wonders, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:5: to Him who made the heavens with understanding, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:6: to Him who established the earth upon the water, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:7: to Him who alone made great lights, for His mercy is forever,
verses.135:8: the sun for authority over the day, for His mercy is forever,
verses.135:9: the moon and the stars for authority over the night, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:10: to Him who struck Egypt with their firstborn, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:11: and brought Israel out from their midst, for His mercy is forever,
verses.135:12: with a mighty hand and with an uplifted arm, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:13: to Him who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:14: and led Israel through its midst, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:15: and shook Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:16: to Him who led His people through the wilderness, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:17: to Him who struck great kings, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:18: and killed mighty kings, for His mercy is forever,
verses.135:19: Sihon king of the Amorites, for His mercy is forever,
verses.135:20: and Og king of Bashan, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:21: and gave their land as an inheritance, for His mercy is forever,
verses.135:22: an inheritance to Israel His servant, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:23: For in our humiliation the Lord remembered us, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:24: and He redeemed us from the hand of our enemies, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:25: He who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:26: Give thanks to the Lord of heaven, for His mercy is forever.
verses.136:1: For David. Beside the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept as we remembered Zion.
verses.136:2: On the willows in its midst we hung our musical instruments.
verses.136:3: For there those who took us captive asked us for words of songs, and those who led us away said, "Sing for us from the songs of Zion."
verses.136:4: How can we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?
verses.136:5: If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be forgotten.
verses.136:6: May my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you, if I do not place Jerusalem first at the head of my gladness.
verses.136:7: Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, those who said, "Empty it, empty it, down to the foundation in it."
verses.136:8: Daughter of Babylon, you wretched one, blessed is the one who will repay you your repayment that you repaid to us;
verses.136:9: blessed is the one who will seize and dash your infants against the rock.
verses.137:1: For David. I will give thanks to You, Lord, with my whole heart, because You heard the words of my mouth; and before angels I will sing praise to You.
verses.137:2: I will bow down toward Your holy temple, and I will give thanks to Your name for Your mercy and Your truth, because You magnified Your holy name above everything.
verses.137:3: On whatever day I call out, hear me quickly; You will care greatly for me in my soul with much strength.
verses.137:4: Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to You, Lord, because they heard all the words of Your mouth;
verses.137:5: and let them sing in the ways of the Lord, for the glory of the Lord is great;
verses.137:6: for the Lord is high, and He looks upon what is lowly, and what is high He knows from afar.
verses.137:7: If I walk in the midst of affliction, You will keep me alive; against the wrath of enemies You stretched out my hands, and Your right hand saved me.
verses.137:8: Lord, You will repay on my behalf; Lord, Your mercy is forever; Lord, do not overlook the works of Your hands.
verses.138:1: For the end; a psalm for David. Lord, You have examined me and known me;
verses.138:2: You have known my sitting down and my rising up; You have understood all my thoughts from afar;
verses.138:3: You have traced out my path and my measuring line, and You have foreseen all my ways,
verses.138:4: because there is no unjust word on my tongue; look, Lord, You have known all things,
verses.138:5: the last things and the ancient things; You formed me and placed Your hand upon me.
verses.138:6: Your knowledge has become wondrous beyond me; it has grown strong; I will by no means be equal to it.
verses.138:7: Where can I go from Your Spirit? And from Your presence where can I flee?
verses.138:8: If I ascend into heaven, You are there; if I descend into Hades, You are present;
verses.138:9: if I take up my wings straight ahead and dwell at the farthest parts of the sea,
verses.138:10: for even there Your hand will guide me, and Your right hand will hold me fast.
verses.138:11: And I said, "Surely darkness will trample me, and night is illumination in my delight."
verses.138:12: As its darkness is, so also is its light.
verses.138:13: For You acquired my inward parts, Lord; You took hold of me from my mother's womb.
verses.138:14: I will give thanks to You, because You have been shown fearfully wondrous; wondrous are Your works, and my soul knows it very well.
verses.138:15: My bone was not hidden from You, which You made in secret, nor my substance in the lowest parts of the earth.
verses.138:16: My eyes saw Your unfinished work, and in Your book all will be written; by day they will be formed, and no one is among them.
verses.138:17: But to me Your friends have been exceedingly honored, God; their dominions have grown exceedingly strong;
verses.138:18: I will count them, and they will be multiplied beyond sand; I awoke, and I am still with You.
verses.138:19: If You would kill sinners, God! Men of blood, turn away from me.
verses.138:20: Because You will speak concerning a thought; they will take Your cities in vain.
verses.138:21: Did I not hate those who hate You, Lord, and waste away over Your enemies?
verses.138:22: With complete hatred I hated them; they became enemies to me.
verses.138:23: Examine me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my paths;
verses.138:24: and see if You have seen lawless deeds in me, and guide me in an eternal way.
verses.139:1: For the end; a psalm for David.
verses.139:2: Rescue me, Lord, from an evil person; deliver me from an unjust man,
verses.139:3: who planned injustices in their heart; all day long they were marshaling wars;
verses.139:4: they sharpened their tongue like that of a serpent; venom of asps is under their lips. Interlude.
verses.139:5: Guard me, Lord, from the hand of a sinner; rescue me from unjust people, who planned to trip up my steps;
verses.139:6: arrogant ones hid a snare for me, and they stretched out cords, snares for my feet; beside the path they set a stumbling block for me. Interlude.
verses.139:7: I said to the Lord, "You are my God." Give ear, Lord, to the voice of my supplication.
verses.139:8: Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, You overshadowed my head in the day of war.
verses.139:9: Do not hand me over, Lord, away from my desire to a sinner; they plotted against me; do not abandon me, so that they may never be exalted. Interlude.
verses.139:10: As for the head of their encirclement, the trouble of their lips will cover them.
verses.139:11: Coals of fire will fall upon them on the earth, and You will cast them down. In miseries they will by no means endure.
verses.139:12: Evils will hunt down an unjust man to destruction.
verses.139:13: I know that the Lord will carry out the judgment of the poor and the justice of the needy.
verses.139:14: Surely righteous ones will give thanks to Your name, and upright ones will dwell in Your presence.
verses.140:1: A psalm for David. Lord, I cried out to You; hear me; pay attention to the voice of my supplication when I cry out to You.
verses.140:2: Let my prayer be directed as incense before You, the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice.
verses.140:3: Lord, set a guard over my mouth and a door of enclosure around my lips.
verses.140:4: Do not turn my heart aside to words of wickedness, to make excuses in sins with people who work lawlessness, and I will never associate with their chosen ones.
verses.140:5: A righteous one will discipline me in mercy and reprove me, but let the oil of a sinner not anoint my head; for yet again and again my prayer is in their pleasures.
verses.140:6: Their strong ones were swallowed up beside a rock; they will hear my words, because they prevailed.
verses.140:7: As a clod of earth was broken apart upon the earth, our bones were scattered beside Hades.
verses.140:8: For toward You, Lord, Lord, are my eyes; in You I have hoped; do not take away my soul.
verses.140:9: Guard me from the snare that they set up for me, and from the stumbling blocks of those who work lawlessness.
verses.140:10: Sinners will fall into his net; I am alone until I pass by.
verses.141:1: Of understanding, for David, when he was in the cave; a prayer.
verses.141:2: With my voice I cried out to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord.
verses.141:3: I will pour out my supplication before Him; my affliction I will declare before Him.
verses.141:4: When my spirit was failing from me, then You knew my paths; in this way in which I was walking, they hid a snare for me.
verses.141:5: I was looking closely to the right and watching, for there was no one who recognized me; escape perished from me, and there is no one who inquires after my soul.
verses.141:6: To You, Lord, I cried out, and I said, "You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living."
verses.141:7: Pay attention to my supplication, for I have been brought very low; rescue me from those who pursue me, for they have grown stronger than me.
verses.141:8: Bring my soul out of prison, so that I may give thanks to Your name, Lord; righteous ones will wait for me until You repay me.
verses.142:1: A psalm for David, when his son pursues him. Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication in Your truth; listen to me in Your righteousness.
verses.142:2: And do not enter into judgment with Your servant, for no one living will be justified before You.
verses.142:3: He brought my life low to the ground; he made me sit in dark places like the dead of long ago.
verses.142:4: And my spirit grew despondent upon me; within me my heart was troubled.
verses.142:5: I remembered ancient days, and I meditated on all Your works; on the deeds of Your hands I kept meditating.
verses.142:6: I spread out my hands to You; my soul is like a waterless land for You. Interlude.
verses.142:7: Hear me quickly, Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn Your face away from me, or I will be made like those who descend into the pit.
verses.142:8: Make me hear Your mercy in the morning, for in You I have hoped; make known to me, Lord, the way in which I will walk, for to You I have lifted up my soul.
verses.142:9: Deliver me from my enemies, Lord, for to You I have fled for refuge.
verses.142:10: Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God; Your Holy Spirit will guide me in the straight way.
verses.142:11: For the sake of Your name, Lord, You will keep me alive in Your righteousness; You will bring my soul out of affliction.
verses.142:12: And in Your mercy You will wipe out my enemies, and You will destroy all those who afflict my soul, for I am Your servant.
verses.143:1: For David, against Goliath. Blessed is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle, my fingers for war,
verses.143:2: my mercy and my refuge, my supporter and my deliverer, my defender, and in Him I have hoped; the One who subjects my people under me.
verses.143:3: Lord, what is man that You were made known to him, or a son of man that You consider him?
verses.143:4: Man has become like emptiness; his days pass by like a shadow.
verses.143:5: Lord, bow Your heavens and come down; touch the mountains, and they will smoke.
verses.143:6: Flash lightning, and You will scatter them; send out Your arrows, and You will throw them into confusion.
verses.143:7: Send out Your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me out of many waters, out of the hand of sons of foreigners,
verses.143:8: whose mouth has spoken emptiness, and their right hand is a right hand of unrighteousness.
verses.143:9: God, I will sing a new song to You; on a ten-stringed harp I will make melody to You,
verses.143:10: to Him who gives salvation to kings, to Him who redeems David His servant. From an evil sword
verses.143:11: deliver me, and rescue me out of the hand of sons of foreigners, whose mouth has spoken emptiness, and their right hand is a right hand of unrighteousness;
verses.143:12: whose sons are like young plants grown sturdy in their youth, their daughters beautified, adorned all around as a likeness of a temple;
verses.143:13: their storehouses are full, pouring forth from this into that; their sheep are prolific, multiplying in their goings-out,
verses.143:14: their oxen are fat; there is no collapse of a fence nor a way out nor an outcry in their courtyards.
verses.143:15: They called the people blessed to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.
verses.144:1: A praise of David. I will exalt You, my God, my King, and I will bless Your name forever, and forever and ever.
verses.144:2: Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name.
verses.144:3: Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no limit to His greatness.
verses.144:4: Generation and generation will praise Your works, and they will declare Your power;
verses.144:5: and they will speak of the majesty of the glory of Your holiness, and they will recount Your wonders;
verses.144:6: and they will tell of the power of Your awesome deeds, and Your greatness, I will recount it, and they will speak of Your might.
verses.144:7: They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of Your goodness, and they will exult in Your righteousness.
verses.144:8: Compassionate and merciful is the Lord, patient and abundant in mercy.
verses.144:9: Good is the Lord to those who endure, and His compassions are over all His works.
verses.144:10: Let all Your works give thanks to You, Lord, and let Your devout ones bless You.
verses.144:11: They will tell of the glory of Your kingdom, and they will speak of Your might,
verses.144:12: to make known to the sons of men Your might and the glory of the majesty of Your kingdom.
verses.144:13: Your kingdom is a kingdom of all the ages, and Your dominion is in every generation and generation. Faithful is the Lord in His words, and holy in all His works.
verses.144:14: The Lord supports all who are falling, and raises up all who are cast down.
verses.144:15: The eyes of all hope in You, and You give their food at the proper time.
verses.144:16: You open Your hands, and fill every living creature with goodwill.
verses.144:17: Righteous is the Lord in all His ways, and holy in all His works.
verses.144:18: Near is the Lord to all who call on Him, to all who call on Him in truth.
verses.144:19: He will do the will of those who fear Him, and He will hear their supplication and save them.
verses.144:20: The Lord keeps all who love Him, and He will utterly destroy all the sinners.
verses.144:21: My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless His holy name forever, and forever and ever.
verses.145:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Praise the Lord, my soul.
verses.145:2: I will praise the Lord in my life; I will make melody to my God as long as I exist.
verses.145:3: Do not trust in rulers and in sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.
verses.145:4: His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; in that day all their thoughts will perish.
verses.145:5: Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob; his hope is in the Lord his God,
verses.145:6: who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them; who keeps truth forever,
verses.145:7: executing justice for those who are wronged, giving food to those who are hungry. The Lord frees those who are shackled.
verses.145:8: The Lord raises up those who are cast down; the Lord makes the blind wise; the Lord loves the righteous.
verses.145:9: The Lord keeps the proselytes; He will uphold an orphan and a widow, and He will wipe out the way of sinners.
verses.145:10: The Lord will reign forever, your God, Zion, to generation and generation.
verses.146:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good; may praise be sweet to our God.
verses.146:2: The Lord is building Jerusalem, and He will gather together the dispersions of Israel.
verses.146:3: He is the One who heals those who are crushed in heart and binds up their fractures.
verses.146:4: He is the One who numbers multitudes of stars and calls all of them by name.
verses.146:5: Great is our Lord, and great is His strength, and there is no number to His understanding.
verses.146:6: The Lord lifts up the meek, but brings sinners low to the ground.
verses.146:7: Begin with thanksgiving to the Lord, sing psalms to our God on a lyre,
verses.146:8: to the One who clothes heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass spring up on mountains, and green vegetation for the service of people,
verses.146:9: and who gives to the livestock their food and to the young of the ravens that call upon Him.
verses.146:10: He will not delight in the power of the horse, nor does He take pleasure in the legs of a man.
verses.146:11: The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear Him, and in all those who hope in His mercy.
verses.147:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Extol the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion,
verses.147:2: for He strengthened the bars of your gates; He blessed your sons within you.
verses.147:3: He is the One who makes your borders peace and fills you with the choicest of wheat.
verses.147:4: He is the One who sends out His utterance to the earth; very swiftly will run the word of Him
verses.147:5: who gives snow like wool, who sprinkles mist like ashes,
verses.147:6: who casts His ice like morsels; in the face of His cold, who will stand?
verses.147:7: He will send out His word and will melt them; His wind will blow, and waters will flow.
verses.147:8: He proclaims His word to Jacob, His ordinances and judgments to Israel.
verses.147:9: He did not do so for any nation, and He did not reveal His judgments to them.
verses.148:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise Him in the highest places.
verses.148:2: Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His powers.
verses.148:3: Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all the stars and the light.
verses.148:4: Praise Him, heavens of the heavens, and the water that is above the heavens.
verses.148:5: Let them praise the name of the Lord, for He Himself spoke and they came into being; He Himself commanded and they were created.
verses.148:6: He established them forever, and forever and ever; He set a decree, and it will not pass away.
verses.148:7: Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all depths;
verses.148:8: fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind, which do His word;
verses.148:9: mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars;
verses.148:10: wild animals and all livestock, creeping things and winged birds;
verses.148:11: kings of the earth and all peoples, rulers and all judges of the earth;
verses.148:12: young men and virgins, old men with younger ones;
verses.148:13: let them praise the name of the Lord, for His name alone has been exalted; thanksgiving to Him is over earth and heaven.
verses.148:14: And He will exalt the horn of His people, for the sons of Israel, a people drawing near to Him.
verses.149:1: Hallelujah. Sing to the Lord a new song; His praise is in the assembly of the devout.
verses.149:2: Let Israel be glad in the One who made him, and let the sons of Zion exult in their King.
verses.149:3: Let them praise His name with dancing; with tambourine and harp let them make music to Him.
verses.149:4: For the Lord takes pleasure in His people, and He will exalt the meek with salvation.
verses.149:5: The devout will boast in glory, and they will exult on their beds.
verses.149:6: The exaltations of God are in their throats, and two-edged swords are in their hands,
verses.149:7: to carry out vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples,
verses.149:8: to bind their kings with fetters and their honored ones with iron manacles,
verses.149:9: to carry out on them a written judgment. This is glory for all His devout ones.
verses.150:1: Hallelujah. Praise God in His holy places; praise Him in the expanse of His power.
verses.150:2: Praise Him for His mighty deeds; praise Him according to the abundance of His greatness.
verses.150:3: Praise Him with the sound of a trumpet; praise Him with harp and lyre.
verses.150:4: Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and a musical instrument.
verses.150:5: Praise Him with clear-sounding cymbals; praise Him with cymbals of jubilation.
verses.150:6: Let every breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah.
verses.151:1: This psalm is written in David's own hand and is outside the number, when he fought in single combat against Goliath. I was small among my brothers and the youngest in my father's house; I was shepherding my father's sheep.
verses.151:2: My hands made a musical instrument; my fingers tuned a harp.
verses.151:3: And who will tell my Lord? The Lord Himself, He Himself hears.
verses.151:4: He Himself sent out His messenger, and took me from my father's sheep, and anointed me with the oil of His anointing.
verses.151:5: My brothers were handsome and tall, and the Lord did not take pleasure in them.
verses.151:6: I went out to meet the foreigner, and he cursed me by his idols.
verses.151:7: But I drew the sword from him, beheaded him, and took away reproach from the sons of Israel.

notes.1:1: Greek loimon ("pestilent ones") literally refers to plagues and is used in the Septuagint for corrupt, destructive people, whereas the Hebrew text reads "scoffers."
notes.1:4: Unlike the Hebrew text, the Greek repeats "not so" for emphasis, uses chnous ("fine dust" or "chaff"), and adds "from the face of the earth."
notes.1:5: Greek boule ("council") is the same word rendered "counsel" in 1:1, carrying both the sense of advice and of a deliberative assembly; anastesontai literally means "will rise" rather than Hebrew "will stand."
notes.2:2: Greek diapsalma ("Interlude") is a musical term indicating a pause or instrumental interlude, corresponding to the Hebrew term Selah (also in 3:3, 3:5).
notes.2:6: The Greek verb is passive ("was established by Him"), making the anointed ruler the speaker rather than God as in the Hebrew text; this Greek witness also omits the word "king" found in some manuscripts.
notes.2:7: Pronouns and "Son" for the speaker (here and in vv. 8-9) are capitalized following traditional messianic reading; in Greek script no uppercase/lowercase distinction exists, and the same speaker is introduced as "His anointed" (2:2) and "king" (2:6).
notes.2:9: Greek poimaneis means "you will shepherd" (echoed in Revelation 2:27; 12:5; 19:15), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants than the traditional Hebrew "you will break."
notes.2:12: Greek draxasthe paideias ("Take hold of instruction") and "from the righteous way" follow the Septuagint wording, differing from the traditional Hebrew ("Kiss the son" and "in the way").
notes.3:1: In Septuagint versification, the psalm's superscription is counted as verse 1, advancing the remaining verse numbers by one relative to most English translations based on the Hebrew.
notes.3:3: This Greek text omits the pronoun auto ("for him") present in some Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew text, reading simply "There is no salvation in his God."
notes.3:4: Greek antilemptor ("sustainer" or "protector") replaces the Hebrew metaphor "a shield around me" and echoes the cognate verb antilempsetai ("will sustain") in 3:6.
notes.3:8: Greek mataios ("without cause" or "groundlessly") differs from the Hebrew text, which reads "on the cheek/jaw."
notes.4:1: "For the end" translates the Greek superscription phrase eis to telos, the Septuagint's standard rendering of the Hebrew musical directive (often translated "for the choir director"). Likewise, "with psalms" renders en psalmois where the Hebrew specifies stringed instruments.
notes.4:3: "Heavy-hearted" (barykardioi) reflects the Greek reading where the Hebrew has "my honor turned to shame." "Interlude" translates diapsalma, the Septuagint term for Hebrew selah, indicating a musical pause.
notes.4:7: "Has been marked upon us" translates the Greek passive indicative esemeiothe ("signed" or "stamped"), contrasting with the Hebrew imperative "lift up."
notes.4:8: Following the Greek text, "and oil" is included alongside grain and wine, and the final verb is third-person plural passive ("they were multiplied") rather than a comparative clause as in the Hebrew.
notes.5:1: "Concerning her who inherits" renders the Greek feminine participle hyper tes kleronomouses, where the Septuagint connects the obscure Hebrew musical term (hannechiloth) to the root for inheriting.
notes.5:9: The Greek text reads "my way before You," reversing the possessive pronouns compared to the Hebrew ("Your way before me").
notes.5:10: The final verb is a Hellenistic imperfect form (edoliousan, "they practiced deceit"); Paul quotes the second half of this verse directly from the Septuagint in Romans 3:13.
notes.5:13: The Greek reads first-person plural "You have crowned us" (estephanosas hemas), whereas the Hebrew has third-person singular "You surround him."
notes.6:1: "Concerning the eighth" (hyper tes ogdoes) translates the Hebrew musical term al-hasheminith, likely referring to an eight-stringed instrument or a lower pitch register.
notes.6:6: "Hades" is the Septuagint's Greek rendering of Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead. "Give thanks to You" translates exomologesetai soi, which carries the sense of open acknowledgment, praise, or confession.
notes.6:8: The Greek reads "because of wrath" (apo thymou, echoing 6:2) rather than Hebrew "grief," and shifts to first-person singular "I have grown old among all my enemies" where the Hebrew keeps "my eye" as the subject.
notes.6:11: All four verbs in the Greek are aorist passive optatives expressing a wish ("May..."), and the Greek repeats sphodra ("greatly") before dia tachous ("swiftly").
notes.7:1: The Greek reads "Chusi son of Jemini" (Chousei son of Iemenei), corresponding to "Cush, a Benjamite" in the Hebrew text.
notes.7:5: Following the Greek, the second clause begins the self-curse ("then may I fall away from my enemies empty"), whereas the Hebrew text reads a further condition ("or plundered my adversary without cause").
notes.7:11: The Greek attaches "Righteous" to the start of v. 11 modifying "my help" (where Hebrew has "my shield"), whereas the Hebrew places "righteous" at the end of v. 10 modifying "God." In v. 10, "kidneys" is the literal idiom for the innermost seat of emotion and conscience.
notes.7:12: The Greek reads "strong and patient, not bringing wrath each day," contrasting with the Hebrew text ("a God who has indignation every day").
notes.8:1: "For the end" (eis to telos) and "concerning the winepresses" (hyper ton lenon) reflect the Greek rendering of Hebrew musical rubrics usually understood as "for the choirmaster" and "according to the Gittith."
notes.8:3: The Greek reads "You have prepared praise" (quoted in Matthew 21:16), whereas the Hebrew text reads "You have established strength."
notes.8:6: The Greek reads "than angels" (quoted in Hebrews 2:7), where the Hebrew has Elohim ("God" or "heavenly beings"). The Greek phrase brachy ti can mean either "a little" in rank or "for a little while" in duration.
notes.9:1: "Concerning the hidden things of the son" reflects the Greek understanding of the obscure Hebrew heading al-mut labben.
notes.9:7: The Greek reads "swords" where the Hebrew text has "ruins," and "with a sound" (met' echous) where the Hebrew has an emphatic pronoun ("they themselves").
notes.9:17: Greek ode diapsalmatos ("Song of an interlude") is the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical rubric Higgaion Selah.
notes.9:21: The Greek reads "a lawgiver" (nomotheten), understanding the Hebrew term as "teacher/lawgiver" rather than "terror."
notes.9:22: In the Septuagint, Psalm 9 continues here as a single composition; verses 9:22-39 correspond to Psalm 10:1-18 in the Hebrew numbering.
notes.9:36: The Greek text includes "on account of it" (di' auten, feminine referring to "his sin"), indicating that the sinner himself will vanish because of his sin.
notes.10:1: The Septuagint superscription "For the end" (Greek eis to telos) renders a Hebrew musical heading ("for the director") by linking it with completion or finality. The Greek also reads plural "mountains" and "sparrow" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has singular "your mountain" and "bird."
notes.10:2: The Greek reads "in a quiver" (eis pharetran), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "on the bowstring."
notes.10:3: The Septuagint reads "what You established, they have torn down" (ha katērtisō katheilon), addressing God directly, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "if the foundations are destroyed."
notes.10:5: In the Greek text, "the one who loves unrighteousness" is the subject who "hates his own soul" (tēn heautou psychēn), whereas in the Hebrew Masoretic Text God's soul hates the wicked and the lover of violence.
notes.10:7: In the Greek, "uprightness" (euthytēta) is accusative, so "His face" (to prosōpon autou) is the subject; the Hebrew is commonly read with the upright as those who see His face.
notes.11:2: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew with the abstract plural "truths" (hai alētheiai), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly read as "the faithful."
notes.11:3: "With a heart and a heart" literally preserves a Hebraic idiom in the Greek (en kardia kai en kardia) denoting a double or insincere heart.
notes.11:6: The Greek verb "I will set" (thēsomai) leaves its object unexpressed, supplied as "them" from "the poor" and "the needy." The closing clause "I will speak boldly in it" (parēsiasomai en autō) is a distinctive Septuagint rendering differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.11:7: The Greek phrase "tested in the earth" (dokimion tē gē) uses a dative without mentioning a furnace, which appears in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.11:9: The Septuagint reading "according to Your height You have greatly esteemed the sons of men" diverges sharply from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("when vileness is exalted among the sons of men").
notes.12:1: The Greek phrase "to the end" (eis telos) literally echoes the superscription "For the end" and carries the idiomatic sense "completely" or "forever."
notes.12:3: This Greek witness reads "the eyes" (tous ophthalmous) without an explicit possessive pronoun, using the definite article in a possessive sense ("my eyes").
notes.12:6: The final clause "and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord, the Most High" is a Septuagint addition absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (compare Psalm 7:18).
notes.13:1: "For the end" literally renders the Septuagint superscription phrase Εἰς τὸ τέλος, which corresponds to the Hebrew musical heading often rendered "For the choir director."
notes.13:3: The extended indictment of human wickedness from "Their throat is an open tomb" through "in front of their eyes" is a notable Septuagint reading (quoted in Romans 3:13-18) that is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 14:3.
notes.13:5: The clause "where there was no fear" is present in the Septuagint here (matching Psalm 52:6 LXX / 53:5 MT) though absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 14:5.
notes.13:7: "Who will give...?" literally renders the Greek idiomatic wish τίς δώσει (reflecting Hebrew "Oh that...").
notes.14:3: "has not deceived" follows the Greek verb ἐδόλωσεν (referring to deceitful speech), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 15:3 has a verb meaning "slander."
notes.14:4: "to his neighbor" translates the Septuagint reading τῷ πλησίον αὐτοῦ, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 15:4 reads "to his own hurt."
notes.15:1: "A pillar inscription" renders Greek Στηλογραφία, the Septuagint equivalent for the obscure Hebrew psalm heading miktam. The Greek also addresses "Lord" (Κύριε) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "God."
notes.15:2: This Greek text ends the verse after "You are my Lord," without the additional clause ("for You have no need of my good things") found in some Septuagint manuscripts and corresponding to Hebrew Psalm 16:2b.
notes.15:4: The Septuagint reflects distinct readings of the underlying Hebrew here, yielding "weaknesses" (for MT "sorrows"), "after these things they hurried" (for MT "barter for another god"), and "assemble their assemblies of blood" (for MT "pour out their drink offerings of blood").
notes.15:7: "my kidneys" literally renders οἱ νεφροί μου, a biblical idiom for the inward mind, conscience, or seat of reflection.
notes.15:10: "corruption" renders Greek διαφθοράν (as quoted in Acts 2:27), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text word in Psalm 16:10 is often rendered "pit."
notes.16:2: The Greek reads "my eyes" (οἱ ὀφθαλμοί μου) rather than the Hebrew "your eyes," with the plural noun εὐθύτητας ("uprightness").
notes.16:7: In the Greek syntax, "Your right hand" is the dative object of "those who resist" rather than an instrumental phrase ("save by Your right hand").
notes.16:13: The accusative "Your sword" (ῥομφαίαν σου) literally reflects the underlying Hebrew syntax and connects directly into the opening phrase of verse 14 ("from enemies of Your hand").
notes.16:14: This Greek text reads "dismissing from the earth" (ἀπολύων ἀπὸ γῆς, versus the variant ἀπὸ ὀλίγων "from a few") and "pork" (ὑείων, "swine's flesh," contrasting with the variant υἱῶν "sons" and the Hebrew).
notes.17:1: "For the end" (Εἰς τὸ τέλος) is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew superscription often translated "for the choirmaster."
notes.17:21: This Greek textual witness repeats the opening sentence of verse 18 ("He will deliver me from my strong enemies and from those who hate me") before the statement of repayment.
notes.17:32: The Greek repeats "God" (θεός) in both questions where the Hebrew reads "a rock" in the second clause.
notes.17:36: The spelling παιδία here represents παιδεία ("discipline" or "instruction," feminine singular), as confirmed by the feminine pronoun αὐτή; the Greek renders this clause with a doubled statement.
notes.17:46: The Septuagint reads "grew old and limped away from their paths" (ἐπαλαιώθησαν καὶ ἐχώλαναν ἀπὸ τῶν τρίβων αὐτῶν), diverging from the Hebrew "fade away and come trembling out of their fortresses."
notes.18:1: Greek eis to telos ("for the end") is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical heading often translated "for the choir director," and to Dauid is a dative ("for/of David"). In Septuagint numbering, Psalms 18-20 correspond to Psalms 19-21 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.18:5: Greek ho phthongos auton ("their sound") is the Septuagint reading quoted in Romans 10:18, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "their measuring line."
notes.18:6: The Greek reads "In the sun He set His tent" (and gigas, "giant"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "In them He set a tent for the sun" (and "strong man").
notes.18:11: Greek lithon timion polyn ("much precious stone") corresponds to "much fine gold" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (compare 20:4).
notes.18:14: Greek apo allotrion pheisai ("spare ... from strangers") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("keep back ... from presumptuous ones"), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants.
notes.19:4: Greek pianato literally means "make fat" (an idiom for accepting an offering as rich and pleasing), and diapsalma ("Interlude") is the Septuagint musical term corresponding to Hebrew selah.
notes.19:6: Greek megalynthesometha ("we will be magnified," repeated in 19:8) reflects a Septuagint reading distinct from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("we will raise banners" in v. 6 and "we will boast/remember" in v. 8).
notes.19:8: Greek leaves the verb unexpressed in the first clause, carrying the contrast directly into "we will be magnified."
notes.19:10: The Greek reads "Your king" and a second-person imperative addressed to the Lord ("and hear us"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text lacks "Your" and has a third-person verb often rendered "may the King answer us."
notes.20:4: Greek ek lithou timiou ("of precious stone") renders the same Hebrew term translated "fine gold" in the Masoretic Text (compare 18:11).
notes.20:9: The Greek uses two optative wishes, first passive (heuretheie, "may ... be found by") and then active (heuroi, "may ... find"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses active verbs.
notes.20:10: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text (which shifts to the third person, "the Lord in His wrath will swallow them up"), the Septuagint addresses the Lord directly in the vocative ("Lord, in Your anger You will throw them into confusion").
notes.20:13: "Make them a back" literally renders the Greek idiom for putting enemies to flight; in the second clause, Greek en tois periloipois sou ("in Your remnants") and hetoimaseis ("You will prepare") differ from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("with Your bowstrings You will aim").
notes.21:1: The Greek superscription literally reads "For the end" (rendering the Hebrew musical heading) and "concerning the morning aid," where the Septuagint read "aid/strength" rather than the Masoretic Hebrew "doe."
notes.21:2: The Septuagint adds "attend to me" after "God, my God" and reads "the words of my transgressions" where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "the words of my groaning."
notes.21:3: The Greek phrase "not to folly for me" (eis anoian) differs from the Masoretic Hebrew, which reads "there is no rest/silence for me."
notes.21:17: The Greek verb oryxan literally means "they dug" (used here in the sense of boring into or piercing), contrasting with the Masoretic Hebrew reading "like a lion."
notes.21:22: Greek monokeroton literally means "of unicorns" (one-horned beasts), rendering the Hebrew for "wild oxen"; "my lowliness" reflects a different vocalization of the Hebrew read in the Masoretic Text as "You have answered me."
notes.22:1: This is Psalm 23 in the Hebrew numbering; the Greek (Septuagint) numbers it Psalm 22. ποιμαίνει ("shepherds") is a present-tense verb, and οὐδέν με ὑστερήσει has "nothing" as its subject, "nothing will be lacking to me."
notes.22:2: κατεσκήνωσεν means "made to encamp, settled (as in a tent)." ἐξέθρεψεν means "nurtured, reared," which is the Greek's own picture in place of "leads."
notes.22:3: ἐπέστρεψεν means "turned back, brought back," and it is rendered literally. The Greek verbs here are aorists, rendered with the English perfect.
notes.22:4: κακά is plural, "evils." παρεκάλεσαν (aorist) is rendered "have comforted."
notes.22:5: ἐλίπανας means "made rich with oil, anointed lavishly." τὸ ποτήριόν σου μεθύσκον ὡς κράτιστον means "Your cup, intoxicating, like the strongest (or best)." This is the Greek's own wording, which differs from the Hebrew "my cup overflows."
notes.22:6: ἔλεος is rendered "mercy." The final clause has no finite verb in the Greek ("and my dwelling in the house of the Lord"), so "will be" is supplied from the parallel. "For length of days" is kept literal.
notes.23:1: The Septuagint adds the liturgical designation "for the first day of the week" (Sunday), which is not found in the Masoretic Hebrew superscription.
notes.23:6: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew musical term Selah; the Greek also specifies "the God of Jacob" rather than simply "Jacob."
notes.23:7: Greek arate pylas, hoi archontes hymon literally means "Lift up gates, your rulers," taking "gates" as the direct object and translating Hebrew "your heads" as "your rulers."
notes.23:10: "The Lord of powers" translates Greek Kyrios ton dynameon (literally "powers," "forces," or "armies"), the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew title "Lord of hosts" (Sabaoth).
notes.24:8: The Greek verb nomothetesei literally means "will lay down law for" or "give legal instruction to," used in the Septuagint to render Hebrew "instruct."
notes.24:12: In Greek, the subject of the verb "chose" (heretisato) is unstated and could refer either to the God-fearing man ("that he chose") or to the Lord ("that He chose").
notes.24:14: Greek krataioma means "stronghold" (differing from the Masoretic Hebrew "friendship/counsel"), and this Septuagint text includes the additional clause "and the name of the Lord belongs to those who fear Him."
notes.24:21: Where the Masoretic Hebrew has a prayer ("May integrity and uprightness preserve me"), the Septuagint reads personal subjects with a past verb ("Innocent and upright ones clung to me") and adds "Lord."
notes.25:2: Greek "kidneys" (nephroi) denotes the innermost thoughts and emotions in biblical idiom, paired here with "heart."
notes.25:3: Greek euērestēsa reflects the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew "walk" (in the sense of living pleasingly before God) and can be understood either as "have been well-pleasing" or "have been well pleased."
notes.25:6: Greek en athōois is plural ("among the innocent," or possibly neuter plural "in innocence"), contrasting with "the ungodly" in verse 5; verse 7 then reads "to hear" (akousai) rather than Hebrew "to proclaim."
notes.25:12: Greek euthytēs carries both the concrete sense of straightness or level ground and the moral sense of uprightness; the closing clause addresses the Lord directly in the second person ("bless You, Lord").
notes.26:1: The superscription phrase "before being anointed" is characteristic of the Septuagint, and "my illumination and my Savior" (phōtismos ... sōtēr) reflects the Greek nouns directly rather than Hebrew "my light and my salvation."
notes.26:6: Greek ekyklōsa ("I went around") reflects a verbal reading of the Hebrew expression for "around me" at the end of the previous clause, and the Greek uses past aorist verbs here and in verse 5.
notes.26:8: Following the Greek punctuation, "my heart said to You" closes the appeal of verse 7, and the first-person verb exezētēsa ("I have sought out Your face") contrasts with the imperative in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.26:12: Greek "souls" (psychas) reflects a Hebrew idiom for the desires or appetite of one's foes; the final clause ("injustice has lied to itself") is a distinctive Septuagint reading.
notes.26:13: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text's conditional clause ("Unless I had believed..."), the Greek states this directly without "unless," and this text reads the future tense pisteusō ("I will believe").
notes.27:1: Greek reads "my God" (where Hebrew has "my rock") and uses the same verb parasiōpaō ("keep silent") in both clauses.
notes.27:5: Greek shifts to second-person verbs ("You will tear them down and will never build them up") addressing God directly, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses third-person verbs.
notes.27:7: Greek "my flesh flourished anew" and "from my will" are distinctive Septuagint readings compared with Hebrew "my heart exults" and "with my song."
notes.27:8: Greek reads "of His people" (where Hebrew has "to them") and plural sōtēria ("deliverances" or "salvations") of "His anointed one" (christou autou).
notes.28:1: The Greek superscription adds "of the closing festival of the tent" (referring to the concluding assembly of the Feast of Tabernacles), and the verse preserves a double rendering with both "sons of God" and "young rams" (lit. "sons of rams").
notes.28:6: The Greek reads "grind them fine" (contrasting with Hebrew "make them skip"), "the beloved one" (contrasting with Hebrew "Sirion"), and "a young unicorn" (lit. "a son of one-horned animals," the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew re'em, wild ox).
notes.28:9: Greek katartizomenou means "strengthening," "making fit," or "perfecting," whereas the Hebrew reads "causes to calve."
notes.28:10: Greek katoikiei is the future of katoikizō ("settle," "cause to be inhabited," as in 4:9), contrasting with the Hebrew past tense "sat enthroned."
notes.29:1: Greek eis to telos ("For the end") is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical heading often translated "for the choir director."
notes.29:6: The Greek reads "wrath is in His anger," whereas the Hebrew reads "His anger is for a moment."
notes.29:8: The Greek text uses the imperative paraschou ("grant") and reads "to my beauty," whereas the Hebrew reads "You made my mountain stand strong."
notes.29:11: The Greek uses past-tense indicative verbs ("heard," "had mercy," "became"), whereas the Hebrew uses imperatives ("Hear," "be gracious," "be").
notes.29:13: Greek katanugo literally means "be pierced" or "feel sharp grief/compunction," whereas the Hebrew reads "be silent."
notes.30:1: The Greek superscription adds ekstaseos ("of dismay" or "of astonishment"), echoing the psalmist's expression in 30:23.
notes.30:7: The Greek has the second-person verb "You have hated," whereas the Hebrew reads first-person "I hate."
notes.30:11: The Greek reads "in poverty" (contrasting with Hebrew "because of my iniquity"), just as 30:10 reads "in anger" rather than "from grief."
notes.30:16: Greek hoi kleroi mou literally means "my lots" or "my portions," whereas the Hebrew reads "my times."
notes.30:23: Greek dia touto reads "Therefore" (contrasting with Hebrew "Yet"); likewise in 30:24 the Greek reads "seeks out truths" rather than "preserves the faithful."
notes.31:2: The Greek reads "in his mouth," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in his spirit."
notes.31:4: The Greek reads "I was turned into misery while a thorn was driven in," diverging from the Masoretic Text ("my vitality was turned into the drought of summer"). "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, corresponding to Hebrew selah as a musical pause.
notes.31:5: The Greek reads "the ungodliness of my heart," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "the guilt of my sin."
notes.31:9: Greek anxai can be taken either as an imperative ("curb") or as an infinitive ("to curb"). Some interpreters also read "to you" as addressed to God ("to You") rather than to the human addressee of verse 8.
notes.32:5: Greek eleemosyne ("compassion" or "almsgiving") stands where the Masoretic Text reads "righteousness."
notes.32:7: Greek hos askon literally means "as a wineskin," reflecting a different Hebrew vocalization (nod, "wineskin") from the Masoretic Text (ned, "heap").
notes.32:10: The third clause, "and He nullifies the counsels of rulers," is a Septuagint reading not found in the Masoretic Text.
notes.32:15: Greek kata monas means "individually" or "one by one," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "all alike" or "together."
notes.33:1: The Greek reads "altered his face" where the Masoretic Text has "changed his behavior/sanity"; Abimelech appears here as the name or title of the Philistine king called Achish in 1 Samuel 21.
notes.33:5: Greek paroikion means "sojournings" (from Hebrew gur, "sojourn"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "terrors" or "fears."
notes.33:6: The Greek has second-person plural imperatives ("Come near... be enlightened") and "your faces," whereas the Masoretic Text has third-person plural indicatives ("They looked... were radiant... their faces").
notes.33:11: Greek plousioi means "the rich," diverging from the Masoretic Text's "young lions"; the Greek also includes "Interlude" (diapsalma), absent from the Hebrew.
notes.33:22: The Greek reads "The death of sinners is evil" rather than the Masoretic Text's "Evil will put the wicked to death." Greek plemmelesousin (also in v. 23) literally means "will err/offend" and in the Septuagint carries the judicial sense "will incur guilt."
notes.34:3: The Greek literally reads "Pour out a sword" (ἔκχεον ῥομφαίαν) and "close in" (σύνκλεισον), reflecting the Septuagint's distinct rendering of the Hebrew weaponry and blocking imagery.
notes.34:7: The Greek reads "the destruction of their snare" (διαφθορὰν παγίδος αὐτῶν) and "reproached" (ὠνείδισαν), differing from the Hebrew imagery of a hidden pit dug for the psalmist.
notes.34:13: The Greek reads "when they were troubling me" (ἐν τῷ αὐτοὺς παρενοχλεῖν μοι) rather than "when they were sick," and uses a future verb ("will return," ἀποστραφήσεται) in the final clause.
notes.34:20: The Greek reads "to me they were speaking peaceful things" (ἐμοὶ μὲν εἰρηνικὰ ἐλάλουν) and "in anger" (ἐπ᾽ ὀργῇ), contrasting with the Hebrew negative ("they do not speak peace") and "quiet ones of the land."
notes.34:27: In the Greek text, "those who desire" (οἱ θέλοντες) is plural, serving as the subject of "let them say" rather than modifying the singular "Lord."
notes.35:1: The Greek heading "For the end" (Εἰς τὸ τέλος) is the regular Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical superscription.
notes.35:2: Literally, "The lawless one says to sin within himself" (Φησὶν ὁ παράνομος τοῦ ἁμαρτάνειν ἐν ἑαυτῷ), a compressed Septuagint rendering of the opening statement about transgression.
notes.35:3: The pronoun in "before him" (ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ) may refer either to the lawless one in his own sight or to God, and the following infinitive clause ("to find his lawlessness and hate it") is compressed and debated.
notes.35:7: The Greek text reads "righteousness" (ἡ δικαιοσύνη) without a possessive pronoun, though contextually referring to God's righteousness; in v. 8, "as You have multiplied" (ὡς ἐπλήθυνας) continues the sentence from v. 7 and can also be read exclamatorily ("How You have multiplied!").
notes.36:3: Greek reads "you will be pastured on its wealth" (ποιμανθήσῃ ἐπὶ τῷ πλούτῳ αὐτῆς), reflecting a Septuagint rendering distinct from the Masoretic Text's "feed on faithfulness."
notes.36:11: Greek γῆ ("land") can also be rendered "earth," as in the quotation of this verse in Matthew 5:5.
notes.36:20: Greek renders the clause as "at the very moment they were glorified and exalted, vanishing like smoke, vanished," differing markedly from the Masoretic Text's imagery of "the glory of the pastures."
notes.36:22: Greek uses active participles ("those who bless... those who curse") rather than the Hebrew passives ("blessed by... cursed by"); "Him" is understood here as referring to the Lord, though grammatically it could also refer back to the righteous one in verse 21.
notes.36:28: Following the Greek critical text here, ἄμωμοι ἐκδικηθήσονται ("The blameless will be vindicated"); another prominent Septuagint manuscript tradition reads ἄνομοι ἐκδιωχθήσονται ("The lawless will be driven out"), corresponding to the missing ayin line of this acrostic psalm in the Masoretic Text.
notes.37:1: The Septuagint superscription adds "concerning the Sabbath" (περὶ σαββάτου), which is absent from the Masoretic Text; this chapter corresponds to Psalm 38 in Hebrew numbering.
notes.37:8: Greek reads "my soul has been filled with mockeries" (ἡ ψυχή μου ἐπλήσθη ἐνπαιγμῶν), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "my loins are filled with burning."
notes.37:12: Greek reads "drew near and stood opposite me" (ἐξ ἐναντίας μου ἤγγισαν καὶ ἔστησαν), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants for "my plague" as the verb "draw near."
notes.37:18: Greek reads "for scourges" (εἰς μάστιγας) where the Masoretic Text has "for stumbling."
notes.38:1: "For the end" translates the standard Septuagint superscription phrase (Eis to telos), corresponding to "For the choir director" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Psalm 39 in Hebrew numbering).
notes.38:6: The Greek reads "old" (palaias), where the Hebrew has "handbreadths," likely reflecting an inner-Greek shift or wordplay with palaistas ("handbreadths"). "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, corresponding to Hebrew selah.
notes.38:9: The Greek states indicatively, "You have made me a reproach to a fool," rather than the Hebrew negative petition ("Do not make me the reproach of the foolish").
notes.38:12: The Greek reads "like a spider's web [or spider] his soul" (hos arachnen ten psychen autou), whereas the Hebrew has "like a moth what is dear to him."
notes.38:13: The Greek reads "on the earth" (en te ge), whereas the Hebrew has "with you."
notes.39:5: The Greek specifically reads "the name of the Lord" as the object of hope, and "futilities and false frenzies" where the Hebrew refers to the proud and those who turn aside to lies.
notes.39:7: The Greek reads "You fashioned a body for me" (soma de katertiso moi), whereas the Hebrew has "ears you have dug [or opened] for me." This Septuagint wording is quoted in Hebrews 10:5.
notes.39:11: The Greek reads "my righteousness" as the direct object of "Lord, You have known" at the end of v. 10, rather than "Your righteousness" with "I have not hidden" as in the Hebrew.
notes.39:16: "Immediately" translates Greek parachrema (where the Hebrew has "because of their shame"), and "Aha, aha!" renders Greek euge, euge (literally "Well done, well done!"), used here as a mocking taunt.
notes.39:17: The Greek text includes "continually" (dia pantos) twice, modifying both the loving of God's salvation and the continual speaking.
notes.40:3: This Greek text omits the clause "and keep him alive" found in the Hebrew and some Septuagint manuscripts, and reads singular "his enemy" rather than plural "his enemies."
notes.40:8: The Greek joins "together against me" (epi to auto kat' emou) with "spoke" at the end of v. 7 rather than with "All my enemies were whispering" as in the Hebrew.
notes.40:9: The Greek frames the enemies' statement as a question ("Will the one who sleeps not rise up again?"), whereas the Hebrew states declaratively that the one who lies down will not rise again.
notes.40:10: "Treachery" translates Greek pternismon ("tripping up by the heel, supplanting, treachery"), a verbal noun from pterna ("heel"), whereas John 13:18 echoes the verse with "lifted his heel against me."
notes.40:14: "May it be so, may it be so" translates the Greek optative genoito, genoito, rendering the Hebrew "Amen and Amen."
notes.41:1: Septuagint Psalm 41 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 42, with verse numbering offset by one because the superscription is counted as verse 1; "For the end; for understanding" is the standard Greek rendering of the Hebrew heading.
notes.41:6: The Greek divides the final clause of the refrain across verses 6 and 7 ("the salvation of my face / is my God"), reading "my face" as in 41:12 and 42:5.
notes.41:7: "Hermoniim" transliterates the Greek plural form of Hermon (Hermonieim), and "from a small mountain" reflects the Septuagint rendering the Hebrew place name Mizar as the adjective "small."
notes.41:9: The Greek text here reads "He will make it known" (delosei, attested in major uncials such as Vaticanus and Sinaiticus), rather than "His song is with me" as in the Hebrew text and other Greek witnesses.
notes.42:1: Septuagint Psalm 42 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 43 and includes the superscription "A psalm of David," which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.42:3: The Greek uses aorist indicative verbs ("they led me and brought me") rather than the jussive request ("let them lead me and bring me") found in the Hebrew text.
notes.43:13: The Greek reads "there was no abundance in their shouts" (alalagmasin, "shouts" or "war cries"), diverging notably from the Hebrew text's "you made no gain from their prices."
notes.43:19: The Septuagint reads a second-person verb ("yet You turned our paths aside from Your way"), whereas the Hebrew text continues the third-person denial ("nor have our steps turned aside from your way").
notes.43:20: The Greek reads "in a place of affliction" (topo kakoseos), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the place of jackals."
notes.43:27: The Septuagint includes the vocative "Lord" and ends with "on account of Your name," whereas the Hebrew text reads "for the sake of your steadfast love."
notes.44:1: The Greek superscription reads 'for the end' (εἰς τὸ τέλος) and 'concerning those who will be changed' (ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων), corresponding to the Hebrew musical headings 'for the choirmaster' and 'according to Lilies'.
notes.44:5: The Greek imperative ἔντεινον literally means 'stretch tight' or 'press on' (often used of bending a bow), reflecting the Septuagint's reading of the Hebrew consonantal text rather than 'in your majesty'.
notes.44:7: The nominative ὁ θεός is read here as a vocative ('God') addressing the royal figure; pronouns in vv. 7-8 are therefore capitalized. Verses 7-8 are quoted in Hebrews 1:8-9.
notes.44:9: Greek στακτή ('stacte') refers to a fragrant oil or resin of myrrh, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'aloes'.
notes.44:14: The Greek text reads the proper name Ἑσεβών ('Heshbon', attested in Codex Vaticanus [B] and Codex Sinaiticus [א]), where Codex Alexandrinus (A) and other Greek witnesses read ἔσωθεν ('within', matching the Hebrew). In v. 16, Greek ναός literally means 'temple' rather than 'palace'.
notes.45:1: The Greek phrase ὑπὲρ τῶν κρυφίων ('concerning the hidden things') interprets the Hebrew musical heading Alamoth through the root meaning 'hide'.
notes.45:2: The Greek begins with 'Our God' (Ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν) and makes the participle modify 'afflictions' ('afflictions that found us exceedingly') rather than describing God as 'very present'.
notes.45:4: Because 'seas' and 'waters' are plural in Greek, singular αὐτοῦ ('His') refers back to God. Greek διάψαλμα ('Interlude') is the Septuagint equivalent of Hebrew Selah.
notes.45:6: The Greek text reads τῷ προσώπῳ (literally 'with the face', i.e., 'with His presence'), an ancient manuscript reading where other Greek witnesses read τὸ πρὸς πρωί ('toward morning', matching the Hebrew).
notes.45:11: Greek σχολάσατε literally means 'cease from activity' or 'be at leisure' (hence 'be at rest' or 'be still'). In vv. 9-10, the Greek also distinctively reads 'wonders' (τέρατα), 'weapon' (ὅπλον), and 'shields' (θυρεούς).
notes.46:5: The Greek reads 'His inheritance' (αὐτοῦ) and 'the beauty of Jacob' (τὴν καλλονὴν Ἰακώβ) with feminine relative ἣν ('which He loved'), whereas the Hebrew has 'our inheritance' and 'the pride of Jacob'.
notes.46:10: The Greek reads 'with the God of Abraham' (μετὰ τοῦ θεοῦ Ἀβραάμ) rather than 'as the people of the God of Abraham', and employs a plural passive verb (ἐπήρθησαν, 'were lifted up') with 'God's mighty ones of the earth' as subject.
notes.47:1: The Greek superscription adds 'on the second day of the week' (literally 'on the second of the Sabbath'), reflecting the ancient liturgical assignment of this psalm to Monday; this phrase is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.47:9: Greek 'diapsalma' ('Interlude') indicates a musical pause or interlude corresponding to Hebrew 'selah'; 'the Lord of powers' literally renders Greek 'Kyriou ton dynameon.'
notes.47:10: The Greek text here reads 'Your people' (laou sou), whereas some Greek witnesses and the Hebrew Masoretic Text read 'Your temple.'
notes.47:12: The Greek reads 'Judea' (Ioudaias) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'Judah.'
notes.47:15: The Greek text ends at 'forever and ever,' without the concluding clause present in some Greek witnesses ('He will shepherd us forever') and in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('He will guide us...').
notes.48:1: Greek 'For the end' (Eis to telos) is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical superscription usually translated 'For the choir director.'
notes.48:6: Literally 'the lawlessness of my heel,' where the Greek translates the Hebrew word literally as 'heel' rather than 'supplanters'; the plural participles in v. 7 follow in loose apposition.
notes.48:8: The Greek syntax of vv. 8-10 diverges notably from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, reading 'A brother does not redeem; will a man redeem?' and taking 'the price of the redemption of his soul' as a direct object of 'He will not give,' followed by 'he labored forever' in v. 9.
notes.48:15: Greek 'Hades' renders Hebrew 'Sheol'; the Greek also reads 'their help' (boetheia) and 'away from their glory' where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'their form' and 'from their dwelling.'
notes.48:19: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('when you do well for yourself'), the Greek reads third-person 'to him' (auto) and uses psalmic verbs of thanksgiving and divine favor, naturally understood as addressing God (though some read the second person as addressing the hearer of v. 17).
notes.49:5: The Greek reads third-person pronouns ('to Him ... His ... His') rather than the first-person pronouns ('to Me ... My ... My') of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.49:10: Greek 'livestock on the mountains and oxen' reflects reading the Hebrew word behind 'a thousand' (eleph) as 'oxen' (alaphim).
notes.49:11: The Greek reads 'birds of heaven' (Hebrew: 'of the mountains') and 'the beauty of the field' (Hebrew: 'what moves in the field').
notes.49:21: Greek 'you supposed lawlessness' (anomian) reflects reading the Hebrew infinitive 'to be' as a noun meaning iniquity or ruin.
notes.49:23: Greek 'and there is the way' (kai ekei hodos) reflects vocalizing the Hebrew word as 'there' rather than 'sets' or 'orders.'
notes.50:1: Greek "eis to telos" ("For the end") is the Septuagint's standard rendering of the Hebrew musical superscription "lamnatseach" ("for the choir director"), and Psalm 50 in the Greek numbering corresponds to Psalm 51 in the Hebrew MT.
notes.50:6: Greek "en to krinesthai se" ("when You are judged," passive or middle, quoted in Rom 3:4) differs from the Hebrew active "when you judge," and "nikeses" ("prevail") corresponds to Hebrew "be blameless."
notes.50:8: The Greek reads "the unseen and hidden things of Your wisdom You have made clear to me," whereas the Hebrew MT speaks of truth in the inward parts and wisdom taught in the secret place.
notes.50:17: The Greek punctuation joins "Lord" to the end of the preceding clause in 50:16, and "anoixeis" ("You will open") is a future indicative rather than an imperative.
notes.51:2: The Greek names the priest Abimelech, whereas the Hebrew MT reads Ahimelech (cf. 1 Sam 21:1), and calls Doeg "the Idumean" (Ἰδουμαῖον, the Septuagint form for Edomite).
notes.51:3: Greek "anomian" ("lawlessness") differs markedly from the Hebrew MT ("the steadfast love of God"), likely reflecting a different reading or the rare homonymous Hebrew sense "reproach/disgrace."
notes.51:5: Greek "diapsalma" ("Interlude") denotes a musical pause or instrumental interlude, corresponding to Hebrew "selah" (also in 51:7).
notes.51:7: The Greek shifts from the future indicative ("will tear you down") to third-person aorist optatives ("may He pluck you out and banish you"), and reads "from a dwelling" without the possessive "your."
notes.51:9: The Greek has "helper" ("boethon") and "futility" ("mataioteti"), where the Hebrew MT reads "refuge" and "destruction" or "desire."
notes.52:1: Greek "maeleth" transliterates the obscure Hebrew musical term "Mahalath," whose exact meaning is uncertain.
notes.52:5: Greek "brosei artou" ("as a meal of bread," lit. "with an eating of bread") renders the Hebrew idiom "as they eat bread"; "My people" reflects God's voice following verse 3.
notes.52:6: Greek "anthropareskon" ("people-pleasers"; cf. Eph 6:6; Col 3:22) differs sharply from the Hebrew MT ("the one who encamps against you"), and "kateischynthesan" ("they were put to shame") is third-person passive rather than second-person active.
notes.52:7: Greek "tis dosei" ("Who will give...?") literally renders the Hebrew wish idiom "mi yitten" ("Oh, that...!"), and "aichmalosian" specifically means "captivity."
notes.53:2: The Greek verb eipen ("he said") is third-person singular following the plural "the Ziphites," a Septuagint reading that treats the delegation collectively or through a spokesman.
notes.53:5: Greek diapsalma ("Interlude") is the Septuagint musical direction corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.53:9: The Septuagint reads second-person "You delivered" (where the Hebrew MT has third-person "he has delivered"); "looked upon" translates the idiomatic epeiden en, implying looking down in triumph.
notes.54:3: Greek adoleschia ("meditation") can also convey anxious musing or complaining.
notes.54:9: The Septuagint reads oligopsychias ("faintheartedness"), where the Hebrew MT has "rushing wind."
notes.54:15: The Septuagint reads "sweetened meals" (eglykanas edesmata), differing from the Hebrew MT "sweetened counsel/fellowship."
notes.54:21: In the Septuagint, vv. 21-22 differ markedly from the Hebrew MT; "He stretched out His hand in repaying; they profaned His covenant" and "the anger of His face" (v. 22) naturally follow God as the singular antecedent before shifting to the deceitful adversary later in v. 22.
notes.55:1: The Septuagint superscription renders the heading as "concerning the people who have been removed far from the holy things" and translates Hebrew Miktam as "a pillar inscription"; Greek allophyloi ("foreigners") is the Septuagint's standard term for the Philistines.
notes.55:3: This Greek text reads "from the height of the day" (apo hypsous hemeras) in v. 3 and third-person plural "will be afraid" (phobethesontai) in v. 4, whereas other Septuagint witnesses read "by day I will not fear" and the Hebrew MT has "When I am afraid."
notes.55:7: This Greek text reads the first-person singular hypemeina ("I waited in my soul"), whereas other Septuagint witnesses read third-person plural "they waited."
notes.55:8: Greek hyper tou methenos soseis autous ("On account of nothing You will save them") is a distinctive Septuagint reading (differing from the Hebrew MT), often understood ironically or rhetorically.
notes.55:11: This Greek text repeats "in God" (epi to theo) in both clauses, where other witnesses and the Hebrew MT read "in the Lord" in the second clause.
notes.56:1: The superscription phrases "For the end" (eis to telos), "do not destroy" (me diaphtheires), and "for a pillar inscription" (eis stelographian) are characteristic Septuagint renderings of Hebrew psalm headings.
notes.56:2: The Greek reads "I will hope" (elpio) and "lawlessness" (he anomia), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I will take refuge" and "calamities."
notes.56:3: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, denoting a musical pause or interlude in the psalm; "who has done good to me" reflects the Greek participle euergetesanta me.
notes.56:5: The Greek links this verse directly to verse 4 with "and rescued my soul from the midst of young lions," followed by "I lay down troubled" (ekoimethen tetaragmenos), differing from the Masoretic Text.
notes.57:5: The Greek reads thymos ("fury" or "wrath"), reflecting a translation of Hebrew chemah in its sense of anger rather than "venom."
notes.57:6: The Greek phrase pharmakou te pharmakeuomenou para sophou literally refers to a charm or potion being worked or prepared by a wise or skilled person.
notes.57:9: The Greek reads "like wax that has melted" (hosei keros ho takeis) and "fire fell" (epepesen pyr), differing markedly from the Masoretic Text ("like a snail" and "a stillborn child").
notes.57:10: This difficult Greek line literally reads "before your thorns understand the bramble," rendering terms for pots and thornbush with two words for thorny plants.
notes.57:11: The Greek explicitly specifies vengeance "on the ungodly" (asebon) and reads "his hands" (tas cheiras autou) rather than "his feet" as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.58:5: In the Greek, both verbs ("I ran and kept a straight course," edramon kai kateuthyna) are first-person singular declarations of the speaker's innocence rather than third-person descriptions of his enemies.
notes.58:6: "Lord God of powers" literally renders Kyrie ho theos ton dynameon, the Septuagint equivalent of "Lord God of hosts" (armies or heavenly powers).
notes.58:12: The Greek reads "Your law" (tou nomou sou), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "my people."
notes.58:13: The Greek clause runs across the boundary of verses 13 and 14, with the passive verb "will be proclaimed" (diangelesontai) in verse 13 governing the plural subject "destructions" (synteleiai) in verse 14.
notes.58:16: This Greek text lacks a negative before "satisfied" ("if they are satisfied, they will also grumble"), whereas some other Septuagint witnesses include "not"; "grumble" (gongysousin) also differs from the Masoretic Text's "spend the night."
notes.59:2: Greek reads 'set fire to' (where Hebrew has 'fought with'), uses the Septuagint form 'Sobal' for Hebrew Zobah (and 'Mesopotamia of Syria' for Aram-naharaim), and reads 'struck the Valley of Salt' without the Hebrew mention of Edom.
notes.59:3: Greek reads the past indicative 'had compassion on us' rather than the Hebrew petition 'restore us.'
notes.59:6: Greek 'from before the bow' reflects reading Hebrew 'truth' (qoshet) as 'bow' (qeshet). 'Interlude' renders Greek diapsalma, the Septuagint equivalent of Hebrew Selah.
notes.59:8: Greek translates the place name Hebrew 'Succoth' literally as 'Tents' (skenon).
notes.59:10: Greek reads 'basin of My hope' (for Hebrew 'my washbasin'), uses 'Idumea' (the Greek name for Edom), and renders Hebrew 'Philistia' as 'foreigners' (allophyloi) with 'have been subjected' rather than Hebrew 'shout in triumph.'
notes.60:2: The Greek critical text omits the vocative 'O God' found in some manuscripts and in the Hebrew text.
notes.60:3: Greek reads two past indicatives ('On a rock You lifted me up; You guided me') rather than the Hebrew petition ('Lead me to the rock that is higher than I').
notes.60:5: The Greek critical text places 'Interlude' (diapsalma) in the middle of the verse rather than at the end as in the Hebrew text.
notes.60:8: Greek reads the question 'who among them will seek out His mercy and truth?' (including the genitive plural pronoun auton) where the Hebrew text reads a petition to appoint steadfast love and faithfulness to preserve the king.
notes.61:2: Greek opens with a rhetorical question ('Will not my soul be subject to God?') where the Hebrew text states 'For God alone my soul waits in silence.'
notes.61:5: Greek reads 'they ran in thirst' where the Hebrew text reads 'they delight in falsehood.'
notes.61:9: Greek reads 'all the congregation of the people' (reflecting Hebrew edah, 'congregation') rather than Hebrew 'at all times, O people' (et, 'time').
notes.61:10: Greek repeats 'the sons of men' in both clauses (where Hebrew contrasts men of low and high degree), reads 'to do injustice' (instead of Hebrew 'to go up'), and renders Hebrew 'lighter than breath' as 'of futility.'
notes.62:1: Greek reads "Idumea" (Ἰδουμαίας), whereas the Hebrew MT reads "Judah."
notes.62:2: Greek "how many times" (ποσαπλῶς) reflects reading the Hebrew verb for "long/faint" as the interrogative "how many/often."
notes.62:3: Greek has the passive "I have appeared to You" (ὤφθην σοι), whereas the Hebrew MT has the active "I have looked upon You."
notes.62:7: Greek "If" (εἰ) renders a Hebrew conditional-temporal particle ("when/whenever"), and "in my early morning" (ἐν τῷ ὄρθρῳ μου) differs from the Hebrew MT's "in the night watches."
notes.62:10: Greek "in vain" (εἰς μάτην) differs from the Hebrew MT's "for destruction/ruin."
notes.63:1: Greek "For the end" (εἰς τὸ τέλος) is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew heading lamnatseach ("to the leader").
notes.63:3: Greek has the past indicative "You have sheltered me" (ἐσκέπασας), whereas the Hebrew MT has the imperative "Hide me."
notes.63:7: Greek "searching out with a search" renders a Hebrew cognate expression for diligent searching, and "a person will draw near" (προσελεύσεται) reads the Hebrew noun for "inward part" as the verb "draw near."
notes.63:8: Greek "God will be exalted" (ὑψωθήσεται) and "an arrow of infants" (βέλος νηπίων) diverge from the Hebrew MT, where God shoots an arrow at them suddenly.
notes.63:9: Greek "despised him" (ἐξουθένησαν αὐτόν) retains a singular pronoun matching the Hebrew collective singular, referring either to each enemy or to their target.
notes.64:3: Greek has the imperative "Hear my prayer" (εἰσάκουσον προσευχῆς μου), whereas the Hebrew MT has a participial address, "O You who hear prayer."
notes.64:6: Greek joins "marvelous in righteousness" to the temple from v. 5 and follows with the imperative "Answer us" (ἐπάκουσον), differing from the Hebrew MT ("By awesome deeds in righteousness You answer us"); this Greek text also ends at "the ends of the earth."
notes.64:8: Greek "troubles" (συνταράσσων) and "The nations will be troubled" diverge from the Hebrew MT, which speaks of God stilling the roaring of the seas and the tumult of the peoples.
notes.64:12: Greek "You will bless the crown of the year of Your goodness" brings the verb "bless" from v. 11 and treats "crown" as a noun, whereas the Hebrew MT reads "You crown the year with Your goodness."
notes.64:14: Greek "The rams of the sheep have clothed themselves" renders a Hebrew word that can mean either "rams" or "meadows," the latter yielding the MT sense "the meadows clothe themselves with flocks."
notes.65:1: The Septuagint superscription adds "of resurrection" (anastaseos), which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.65:5: The Greek text includes the vocative "children" (tekna), a reading found in several Septuagint witnesses though absent from the Hebrew text.
notes.65:11: The Greek text reads "before us" (enopion hemon), a Septuagint variant differing from witnesses (and the Hebrew text) that read "upon our back."
notes.65:16: The Greek text here reads "the Lord" (ton kyrion), whereas the Hebrew text and some Septuagint witnesses read "God."
notes.66:1: The Septuagint renders the musical heading as "with hymns" (en hymnois) and attributes the psalm to David, an attribution absent from the Hebrew text.
notes.66:4: Unlike verse 6, the Greek text here omits the pronoun "to You" (soi) in both clauses, a reading preserved in major early Septuagint witnesses.
notes.67:7: Differing from the Hebrew text ("the rebellious dwell in a parched land"), the Septuagint links "those who rebel" with the preceding deliverance and renders the final word as "in tombs" (en taphois).
notes.67:13: The Septuagint diverges markedly from the Hebrew text here, rendering the repeated verb as "of the beloved, of the beloved" (tou agapetou, tou agapetou) and linking "for the beauty of the house" with dividing spoils.
notes.67:16: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew "mountain of Bashan" and "many-peaked mountain" as "a fat mountain" (oros pion) and "a curdled mountain" (oros tetyromenon), imagery echoed in verse 17.
notes.67:19: Unlike the Hebrew text, the Septuagint ends verse 19 at "to take up dwelling" and begins verse 20 with "The Lord God is blessed"; it also reads the singular "in man" (en anthropo).
notes.67:31: The Greek text includes the negative particle me ("may not be shut out"), a reading of major early Septuagint manuscripts differing from witnesses that omit it.
notes.67:36: The Greek text reads "in His devout ones" (en tois hosiois autou), a textual variant alongside Septuagint witnesses that read "in His holy ones/sanctuaries" (en tois hagiois autou).
notes.68:1: The Septuagint superscription reads "concerning those who will be changed" (ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων), interpreting the Hebrew heading ("according to Lilies") from a related root meaning "to change."
notes.68:4: The Greek text reads ἐγγίζειν ("drawing near"), found in major early Septuagint manuscripts, whereas other Greek witnesses read ἐλπίζειν ("hoping") and the Hebrew reads "waiting."
notes.68:10: The Greek text has the future tense καταφάγεταί ("will consume"), matching the quotation in John 2:17, where other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew have a past tense.
notes.68:18: This shorter Greek text omits the opening clause ("and do not turn away Your face from Your servant") found in some Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew.
notes.68:23: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew as ἀνταπόδοσιν ("retribution", cf. Romans 11:9), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "for those at peace" (or "for peace offerings").
notes.69:1: The closing clause of the superscription, "that the Lord may save me" (εἰς τὸ σῶσαί με Κύριον), is distinctive to the Septuagint and does not appear in the Hebrew.
notes.69:2: This shorter Greek text lacks the second clause ("Lord, hasten to help me") present in other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew.
notes.70:1: The superscription associating this psalm with David, the sons of Jonadab, and the first captives is distinctive to the Septuagint; the Hebrew psalm has no superscription.
notes.70:12: This shorter Greek text omits the second clause ("my God, attend to my help") found in other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew.
notes.70:15: The Greek text reads πραγματίας ("business affairs"), a major early Septuagint reading; other Greek manuscripts read γραμματείας ("learning" or "reckoning"), and the Hebrew reads "numbers."
notes.70:21: The Greek text reads τὴν δικαιοσύνην σου ("Your righteousness") where the Hebrew and other manuscripts read "Your greatness," and it retains the repeated closing clause ("and from the abysses You brought me up again") absent from the Hebrew.
notes.71:4: The Greek places 'in righteousness' at the opening of v. 4 rather than v. 3 and reads second-person singular σώσεις ('You will save'), momentarily addressing God directly; συκοφάντην literally denotes a false accuser or extortioner.
notes.71:9: LXX renders Hebrew 'desert-dwellers' as Αἰθίοπες ('Ethiopians'), as also in 73:14, and in v. 10 reads 'kings of the Arabs and Saba' where the Masoretic Text has 'Sheba and Seba.'
notes.71:10: Greek reads "Arabs and Saba," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Sheba and Seba."
