notes.71:14: Greek reads τόκου ('usury') and τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῶν ('their name'), where the Masoretic Text has 'oppression' and 'their blood.'
notes.71:16: Greek reads στήριγμα ('a support'), reflecting a different understanding of the Masoretic Text's 'abundance of grain'; the pronoun αὐτοῦ ('his' or 'its') can refer either to the king or to the support.
notes.72:4: The rare Greek noun ἀνάνευσις denotes throwing back the head in refusal or reluctance, while στερέωμα means 'firmness'; both differ notably from the Masoretic Text.
notes.72:7: Greek reads ἡ ἀδικία αὐτῶν ('their injustice'), whereas the Masoretic Text has 'their eye.'
notes.72:18: This critical text preserves only the first clause of the verse, with the elliptical ἔθου αὐτοῖς (literally 'You set/appointed for them') and διὰ τὰς δολιότητας ('because of the deceits,' corresponding to MT 'in slippery places').
notes.72:21: Greek reads ηὐφράνθη ('was gladdened') and ἠλλοιώθησαν ('were changed'), contrasting with the Masoretic Text's 'was embittered' and 'was pierced'; 'kidneys' (νεφροί) is a literal biblical idiom for the inner being.
notes.72:28: This Greek text reads 'the Lord' twice, 'Your praises' (MT 'Your works'), and includes the closing phrase 'in the gates of the daughter of Zion,' which is absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.73:4: This critical text omits the second clause of v. 4 found in some witnesses ('they set up their signs as signs and did not know'); v. 5 then renders an obscure Hebrew phrase literally as 'as at the entrance above.'
notes.73:9: Greek καὶ ἡμᾶς οὐ γνώσεται ἔτι ('and He will know us no longer') differs from the Masoretic Text ('none among us knows how long'); the unexpressed subject of γνώσεται could refer either to God ('He') or to a prophet ('he').
notes.73:14: This critical text omits the opening clause of v. 14 ('You shattered the heads of the dragon') and the closing clause of v. 15 ('You dried up the rivers of Etham'), leaving αὐτὸν ('him') in v. 14 without an explicit singular antecedent; 'Ethiopian' again renders Hebrew 'desert-dwellers.'
notes.73:19: Greek reads ψυχὴν ἐξομολογουμένην σοι ('a soul that gives thanks to You') where the Masoretic Text has 'the life of your dove.'
notes.73:23: Greek reads τῶν ἱκετῶν σου ('of Your suppliants') where the Masoretic Text has 'of your adversaries,' and uses the optative ἀναβαίη with πρὸς σέ ('may ... ascend to You').
notes.74:2: LXX reads "and call upon Your name" and first-person singular "I will recount" (MT: "Your name is near; they recount").
notes.74:3: Greek punctuation links "when I take an appointed time" with 74:2; "with uprightness" translates the Greek adverbial accusative plural euthytētas (lit. "uprightnesses").
notes.74:4: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, a musical pause or interlude corresponding to Hebrew Selah (similarly in 75:4, 75:10, 76:4, 76:10, and 76:16).
notes.74:7: The Greek sentence is elliptical without an explicit verb and omits "mountains"; "the east" translates exodōn (lit. "goings-out [of the sun]").
notes.74:9: The Greek literally has the paradox "of unmixed wine, full of mixture," uses eklinen (lit. "tilted/inclined") for pouring, and reads "its dregs were not emptied out" (differing from MT).
notes.75:1: LXX adds "concerning the Assyrian" to the superscription (absent from MT), linking the psalm to deliverance from Assyria.
notes.75:4: LXX reads "the powers of the bows" (MT: "flashing arrows"), and the Greek critical text includes the additional clause "there He will break the horns" (absent from MT).
notes.75:6: LXX reads "senseless in heart" and "all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands" (MT: "stouthearted" and "none of the men of might found their hands").
notes.75:9: "You hurled" translates Greek ēkontisas (from akontizō, "hurl/shoot," attested in Sinaiticus), whereas other witnesses read ēkoutisas ("caused to be heard").
notes.75:11: LXX renders the underlying Hebrew as "thought" (enthymion) and "will keep a festival" (heortasei), whereas MT reads "wrath" and "gird Yourself."
notes.76:3: LXX reads "with my hands by night before Him, and I was not deceived" (MT: "in the night my hand was stretched out without growing weary").
notes.76:5: The Greek critical text reads "my enemies" (hoi echthroi mou, supported by Vaticanus and Sinaiticus), whereas other Greek witnesses and MT read "my eyes."
notes.76:9: The Greek critical text follows early uncials (including Vaticanus and Sinaiticus) in omitting "has His promise ended?" and reads literally "to the end ... from generation and generation."
notes.76:11: LXX reads "Now I have begun; this is the change," interpreting the Hebrew differently from MT ("This is my grief/appeal: the years...").
notes.76:19: "In the wheel" translates Greek en tō trochō literally (MT: "in the whirlwind"), and the Greek critical text omits the clause "Your lightnings lit up the world" found in MT and other witnesses.
notes.77:12: Tanis (Greek Taneos) is the Septuagint name for the Egyptian Delta city known as Zoan in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.77:13: The Greek reads "waterskin" (askon, a leather liquid container), reflecting a different reading from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "heap."
notes.77:21: The Greek verb anebaleto literally means "delayed" or "put off," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "was full of wrath."
notes.77:31: The Greek phrase en tois pleiosin auton means "among the majority of them" (compared with Hebrew "among their stoutest ones"). Here and across verses 30-36, the Septuagint verse divisions fall mid-clause.
notes.77:36: The Greek reads "loved" (egapesan), contrasting outward speech with the deceit completed in verse 37, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "flattered" or "deceived."
notes.77:50: The Greek text reads "and He confined their livestock to death," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "and He gave over their life to the plague."
notes.77:63: The Greek reads "did not mourn" (ouk epenthesan), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "were not praised" (i.e., had no wedding songs).
notes.77:64: The Greek verb klausthesontai is future passive ("will not be wept for"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "did not weep."
notes.77:65: The Greek participle kekraipalekos specifically describes one suffering the dazed after-effects or hangover of heavy drinking.
notes.77:69: The Greek reads "like that of unicorns" (hos monokeroton, literally one-horned beasts), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic Text's "like the heights."
notes.78:1: Greek oporophylakion literally means "a fruit-watcher's hut" (a temporary orchard shed), whereas the Hebrew text reads "heaps of ruins."
notes.78:10: The Greek text introduces a negative purpose clause ("so that they may never say among the nations") rather than the Hebrew question "Why should the nations say?"
notes.78:11: Greek tous huious ton tethanatomenon literally means "the sons of those put to death," reflecting a perfect passive participle where the Hebrew idiom "sons of death" refers to those condemned to die.
notes.79:1: The Greek superscription renders the Hebrew heading as "For the end," reads "concerning those who will be changed" where Hebrew has "lilies," and includes the Septuagint-distinct phrase "concerning the Assyrian."
notes.79:5: Greek ton dynameon ("of powers," also used for military forces or hosts) renders Hebrew tseva'ot ("of hosts"); here the Greek also reads "Your servant" where the Hebrew reads "Your people."
notes.79:8: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew selah indicating a musical pause; the Greek text also includes "Lord" here as in verses 5 and 20.
notes.79:14: Greek onos agrios means "a wild donkey," where the Hebrew text reads "whatever moves in the field."
notes.79:16: Greek katartisai ("restore") reads a verb where the Hebrew has a noun ("stock/root"), and the Septuagint reads "the son of man" here just as in verse 18, where the Hebrew has simply "son."
notes.80:1: Greek hyper ton lenon ("concerning the winepresses") renders the Hebrew musical heading haggitit ("the Gittith") from the related Hebrew word for a winepress.
notes.80:4: Greek en eusemo hemera ("on the notable day" or "well-marked day") differs from the Hebrew reading "at the full moon."
notes.80:6: In verses 6-7, the Greek text uses third-person verbs ("heard," "removed") where the Hebrew shifts to first-person speech, and in verse 7 reads edouleusan ("slaved/served") where the Hebrew reads "were freed."
notes.80:8: Greek hydatos Antilogias ("the water of Contention," singular "water") translates the Hebrew place-name "waters of Meribah."
notes.80:16: In verses 16-17, the Greek text uses past-tense verbs ("lied," "fed," "satisfied") and third-person "them" throughout verse 17, rather than continuing the conditional wish or shifting to second-person "you" as in the Hebrew.
notes.81:1: Greek places theous ("gods") in the accusative as the direct object of diakrinei ("judges"), with en meso ("in the midst") standing adverbially, whereas the Hebrew reads "in the midst of the gods He judges."
notes.81:2: Greek prosopa hamartolon lambanete literally means "accept the faces of sinners," a Semitic idiom for showing partiality. Diapsalma ("Interlude") is the Septuagint's rendering of Hebrew selah, indicating a musical pause or interlude.
notes.81:8: Greek katakleronomeseis en pasin tois ethnesin literally means "You will inherit among all the nations," preserving the prepositional phrase rather than making the nations a direct object.
notes.82:2: Greek tis homoiothesetai soi ("who will be likened to You?") reflects reading Hebrew domi from the root meaning "be like" rather than "be silent" (as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, "do not keep silence").
notes.82:4: Greek ton hagion sou ("Your holy ones") stands where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Your treasured ones" (or "hidden ones").
notes.82:8: The Greek text reads Naibal (attested in Codex Vaticanus) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Greek manuscripts read Gebal. Greek allophyloi literally means "foreigners" and is the Septuagint's standard rendering of "Philistines."
notes.82:13: The Greek text reads thysiasterion ("altar"), contrasting with other Greek manuscripts reading hagiasterion ("sanctuary") and the Hebrew Masoretic Text reading "pastures" (or "dwellings").
notes.82:19: Greek Kyrios ("the Lord") here renders the Hebrew divine name (YHWH).
notes.83:1: Greek eis to telos ("For the end") and hyper ton lenon ("concerning the winepresses") are the Septuagint's renderings of the Hebrew headings traditionally understood as "For the choirmaster" and "on the Gittith."
notes.83:7: Greek renders Hebrew "valley of Baca" etymologically as "valley of weeping," reads "to the place that he appointed" (grammatically referring to the pilgrim of v. 6, though sometimes taken of God), and translates Hebrew moreh ("early rain") as ho nomotheton ("the Lawgiver").
notes.83:8: Greek reads ho theos ton theon ("the God of gods") as the subject of passive ophthesetai ("will be seen"), whereas the Hebrew reads "each one appears before God in Zion." The phrase "from power to power" (ek dynameos eis dynamin) also echoes the Greek title "Lord of powers" (ton dynameon, vv. 2, 4, 9, 13, rendering Hebrew tsebaoth).
notes.83:11: Greek has plural chiliadas ("thousands") rather than singular "a thousand," uses pararipteisthai ("to be cast aside") where the Hebrew reads "stand at the threshold," and reads "of God" rather than "of my God."
notes.83:12: Greek reads "loves mercy and truth" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "is a sun and shield." Following the Greek punctuation, "the Lord" begins the final sentence.
notes.84:1: "For the end" translates Greek eis to telos, the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical superscription often translated "for the choir director."
notes.84:3: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, the Septuagint equivalent of Hebrew Selah, indicating a musical pause or interlude.
notes.84:7: Unlike the Hebrew text, which frames this verse as a question ("Will you not revive us again?"), the Greek expresses it as a declarative statement of confident expectation.
notes.84:9: The Greek includes "in me" (en emoi) and concludes with "those who turn their heart toward Him," whereas the Hebrew reads "let them not turn back to folly."
notes.84:14: "Will set His steps on a way" translates Greek thesei eis hodon ta diabemata autou, which can also be rendered idiomatically as "will make His steps into a way."
notes.85:7: Both verbs ("I cried out" and "You heard me") are past-tense aorists in the Greek, contrasting with the present or future sense ("I call ... you answer") in the Hebrew.
notes.85:10: The Greek concludes with the emphatic appositive "the great One" (ho megas), an addition not present in the Hebrew text.
notes.85:11: The Greek reads "Guide me" (hodegeson me) and "let my heart rejoice" (euphrantheto he kardia mou), where the Hebrew reads "Teach me" and "unite my heart."
notes.85:13: "Hades" preserves Greek hades, the standard Septuagint rendering of Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead.
notes.86:1: "His foundations" translates the masculine singular Greek autou, referring to the Lord (v. 2) or, by carryover from the Hebrew suffix, to the sanctuary or city itself.
notes.86:4: "Foreigners" translates Greek allophyloi, the regular Septuagint term for the Philistines, and "the people of the Ethiopians" reflects Greek laos Aithiopon where the Hebrew simply has "Cush."
notes.86:5: Whereas the Hebrew reads "Of Zion it shall be said, 'This one and that one was born in her,'" the Greek reads "'Mother Zion,' a man will say." In this Greek text the capitals on Anthropos and Autos mark the start of quoted words, as elsewhere in the Psalms (e.g., 81:6).
notes.86:6: The Greek adds "and rulers" (kai archonton) and uses the plural "of these who have been born in her," differing from the singular "this one was born there" in the Hebrew.
notes.86:7: The Greek reads katoikia ("dwelling") with a compact comparative genitive ("like that of all who rejoice"), where the Hebrew reads "Singers and dancers alike say, 'All my springs are in you.'"
notes.87:1: The Greek superscription renders the Hebrew heading literally as "for the end," "to answer," and "of understanding," transliterates Mahalath, and calls Heman "the Israelite" (where the Hebrew has "the Ezrahite," and likewise for Ethan in 88:1).
notes.87:7: Greek reads third-person plural "They placed me" here and "they made me" in v. 9 (where the Hebrew has second-person singular "You"). In v. 8, "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, the Septuagint musical direction corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.87:11: Greek reads "physicians" (iatroi), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants for "shades/departed spirits" (rephaim), followed by the active verb "raise [them] up."
notes.87:16: Greek reads "in labors" and "having been exalted, I was humbled and utterly perplexed," diverging markedly from the Hebrew ("about to die; I suffer your terrors; I am helpless"). Similarly, in v. 15 Greek reads "my prayer" where the Hebrew has "my soul."
notes.87:19: Greek closes the psalm with "because of misery" (apo talaiporias), whereas the Hebrew ends with "darkness."
notes.88:3: Greek reads second-person "For You said" (whereas the Hebrew has "For I said") and in v. 4 plural "My chosen ones."
notes.88:13: Greek reads "seas" (thalassas, where the Hebrew has "south") and uses the plural form "Hermoniim" for Mount Hermon; in v. 11, Greek renders Hebrew Rahab as the common term "a proud one."
notes.88:21: Greek reads "with holy mercy" (en eleei hagio) rather than "with My holy oil" (as in the Hebrew and some Greek manuscripts); in v. 20, Greek reads "to Your sons" where the Hebrew has "to your godly ones."
notes.88:45: Greek reads "from purification" (where the Hebrew has "his splendor") and in v. 46 "the days of his throne" (where the Hebrew has "the days of his youth").
notes.88:51: The Greek text reads second-person singular "which You bore" (hypeschou, whereas other Greek witnesses read first-person "which I bore," matching the Hebrew); in v. 52, Greek "recompense" (antallagma) reflects the alternative sense of the Hebrew root for "footsteps."
notes.89:3: Unlike the Hebrew MT ("You return man to dust"), the Septuagint begins with a prohibition ("Do not turn ... back") and reads "humiliation" (tapeinosis); the closing question mark reflects the punctuation of the Greek source text (some editions punctuate the second clause as a statement).
notes.89:5: The Greek reads "Their things of no account will be years," reflecting a Hebrew vocalization meaning "year" rather than MT "sleep," followed by a series of optative verbs ("may it...") in vv. 5-6.
notes.89:9: The closing Greek clause is notoriously difficult: the accusative arachnen can mean "spider" or "spider's web," and the imperfect verb emeleton is ambiguous in form between third-person plural ("our years devised/practiced") and first-person singular ("I pondered our years like a spider's web").
notes.89:10: The Saints Greek text reads en eniautois ("in years," where many Greek manuscripts read en autois, "in them") and follows the Septuagint in reading "for gentleness has come upon us, and we will be disciplined" (differing from the MT).
notes.89:11: The Greek attaches the infinitive exarithmesasthai ("to reckon" or "to number") to v. 11 rather than v. 12 (as in the MT) and reads the genitive phrase "the fear of Your fury."
notes.90:1: The superscription ("A praise of a song, for David") appears in the Septuagint but not the Hebrew MT; the Greek also reads "in the help of the Most High" and "the God of heaven" where the MT has "shelter" and "the Almighty" (Shaddai).
notes.90:3: The Saints Greek text omits "you" after "will rescue" (present in some manuscripts) and follows the Septuagint in reading "hunters" and "a troublesome word" (reading Hebrew dabar "word" rather than MT deber "pestilence").
notes.90:6: The Septuagint reads "a thing" (again reading Hebrew dabar rather than MT deber "pestilence") and "a midday demon," differing from the MT's "destruction that wastes at noonday."
notes.90:11: The Saints Greek text reads simply "in your ways," omitting "all" found in the MT and some other Greek manuscripts.
notes.90:13: Following the Septuagint, the Greek names two venomous serpents ("an asp and a basilisk") where the Hebrew MT has "the lion and the cobra."
notes.91:6: The Saints Greek text reads ebarynthesan ("have become weighty/heavy"), a textual variant where other Greek manuscripts read ebathynthesan ("have become deep," matching the Hebrew MT).
notes.91:8: Greek diekypsan literally means "peered forth" or "peered out," rendering the Hebrew verb for "flourished" by a similarly spelled Hebrew verb meaning "peer out."
notes.91:10: The Saints Greek text has the shorter single clause "For look, Your enemies will perish," without the repeated clause found in the Hebrew MT and some Greek manuscripts.
notes.91:11: Greek monokeros literally means "one-horned creature" or "unicorn" (the standard Septuagint rendering of Hebrew re'em, "wild ox"), and the Septuagint reads "my old age" where the MT has "I have been anointed."
notes.91:15: The Saints Greek text reads tote ("Then") rather than eti ("Still") found in the MT and other Greek manuscripts.
notes.92:1: The Septuagint superscription (absent from the Hebrew MT) assigns this psalm to the day before the Sabbath (Friday), linking it to the completion of creation when the earth was inhabited.
notes.92:3: The Greek text has two clauses with plural "voices," omitting the third clause found in the Hebrew MT.
notes.92:4: Greek ἀπό ("from") renders a Hebrew preposition that can be taken causally ("from") or comparatively ("more than"); μετεωρισμοί refers to the rising swells or surges of the sea.
notes.93:1: The Septuagint superscription assigns this psalm to Wednesday ("the fourth day of the week"), and ἐκδικήσεων is plural ("acts of vengeance"). Greek ἐπαρρησιάσατο ("acted boldly" or "spoke openly") is an aorist indicative, where the Hebrew is usually rendered as an imperative ("shine forth").
notes.93:15: The Greek reverses the Hebrew subject and object so that righteousness returns to judgment, and closes with διάψαλμα ("Interlude"), a liturgical/musical pause corresponding to Hebrew Selah that is absent here in the MT.
notes.93:17: Greek τῷ ᾅδῃ ("in Hades") differs from the Hebrew MT reading "in silence."
notes.93:19: Greek ἠγάπησαν ("loved") is the reading of major Septuagint witnesses, diverging from the Hebrew "delighted/cheered" and later Greek manuscripts that read "gladdened."
notes.93:23: In this Greek text, both "their lawlessness" and "their wickedness" are direct objects of "repay," followed by a single concluding verb "will destroy."
notes.94:4: The opening clause "For the Lord will not reject His people" (echoing 93:14) is a Septuagint reading absent from the Hebrew MT, and πέρατα means "ends" rather than the Hebrew "depths."
notes.94:6: Greek κλαύσωμεν ("let us weep") reflects a reading that differs from the Hebrew MT "let us kneel."
notes.94:8: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew place names Meribah and Massah as common nouns: παραπικρασμός ("provocation/rebellion") and πειρασμός ("testing").
notes.94:11: Greek literally reads "If they will enter into My rest," a Semitic oath idiom expressing an emphatic negative.
notes.95:1: The Greek superscription attributes this psalm to David in connection with the rebuilding of the temple after the exile; Hebrew Psalm 96 has no superscription.
notes.95:5: Greek renders the gods of the nations as "demons" (δαιμόνια), contrasting them with the Lord who made the heavens.
notes.95:9: Greek reads "in His holy court" (ἐν αὐλῇ ἁγίᾳ αὐτοῦ), continuing the temple court imagery from verse 8, where the Hebrew has "in the splendor of holiness."
notes.95:11: Greek uses σαλευθήτω ("be shaken"), echoing the same verb used of the earth in verses 9-10 rather than "roar" as in the Hebrew.
notes.96:1: The Greek superscription ("For David, when his land is being established") has no counterpart in Hebrew Psalm 97. Here and in 95:10, the aorist ἐβασίλευσεν carries an ingressive sense ("has become king").
notes.96:7: Greek reads "all His angels" (πάντες οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτοῦ), corresponding to Hebrew "all gods," a wording echoed in Hebrews 1:6.
notes.96:8: Greek uses the regional name "Judea" (Ἰουδαίας) rather than the tribal or kingdom name "Judah."
notes.96:11: Greek reads "has dawned" (ἀνέτειλεν), reflecting a different understanding of the Hebrew verb usually translated "is sown."
notes.97:1: The Greek superscription adds "for David" (τῷ Δαυίδ), whereas Hebrew Psalm 98 reads only "A psalm." The dative αὐτῷ ("Him") indicates that His right hand and holy arm achieved salvation on His behalf.
notes.97:2: The Greek punctuation joins "before the nations" (ἐναντίον τῶν ἐθνῶν) with the first clause ("made His salvation known") rather than with the second ("revealed His righteousness").
notes.97:3: Greek specifies "His mercy to Jacob" alongside "His truth to the house of Israel," whereas the Hebrew mentions only the house of Israel.
notes.97:6: The Greek critical text reads the dative Κυρίῳ ("to the Lord") after the genitive τοῦ βασιλέως ("before the King"), pairing it with the verb "shout joyfully" as in verse 4.
notes.97:8: Greek places "together" (ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό) with the clapping rivers rather than the exulting mountains, and proceeds directly into verse 9 without the phrase "before the Lord."
notes.98:1: The Septuagint includes the superscription "A psalm for David" (absent in Hebrew Ps 99) and renders the verb as "be angry" (ὀργιζέσθωσαν) rather than "tremble." The aorist ἐβασίλευσεν is ingressive ("has become king" or "reigned").
notes.98:3: The Greek text includes πάντες ("all"), which is absent in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Septuagint witnesses.
notes.98:4: The Septuagint reads τιμὴ βασιλέως ("the honor of a king") where the Hebrew has "the strength of a king," and εὐθύτητας is literally plural ("upright things" or "equities").
notes.98:6: This Greek text omits ὅτι ("for") at the end of v. 5 and places ἅγιός ἐστιν ("He is holy") at the beginning of v. 6, as in major uncials such as Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Punctuated here as an independent refrain referring to the Lord (matching vv. 3 and 9), it could alternatively be read syntactically with the following name ("Holy is Moses...").
notes.99:1: Greek ἐξομολόγησις (like the verb ἐξομολογέω in 98:3 and 99:4) denotes public acknowledgment, confession, or thanksgiving.
notes.99:3: The Septuagint reads καὶ οὐχ ἡμεῖς ("and not we"), agreeing with the Hebrew Ketiv against the Qere ("and His we are").
notes.99:4: The Septuagint reads ἐν ὕμνοις ("with hymns") and αἰνεῖτε ("praise") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "with praise" and "bless."
notes.100:2: This Greek text reads ἐν ᾠδῇ ἀμώμῳ ("in a blameless song") rather than ἐν ὁδῷ ἀμώμῳ ("in a blameless way," as in v. 6 and other witnesses). From διεπορευόμην ("I walked") through v. 8, the Septuagint consistently uses past tenses (imperfect and aorist) where the Hebrew uses future/modal imperfects.
notes.100:4: The Septuagint divides the clauses differently from the Hebrew, using a genitive absolute (ἐκκλίνοντος ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ τοῦ πονηροῦ, "when the evil person [or evil] turned away from me") followed by οὐκ ἐγίνωσκον ("I did not know") with no expressed object (implying "it" or "him").
notes.100:5: Greek οὐ συνήσθιον ("I did not eat with") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("I will not endure"), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants.
notes.100:7: The Septuagint reads ποιῶν ὑπερηφανίαν ("one practicing arrogance") and λαλῶν ἄδικα ("one speaking unjust things") where the Hebrew has "one who practices deceit" and "one who speaks falsehood."
notes.101:4: Greek φρύγιον ("firewood", or in later usage a roasting pan) is a rare term paired with συνεφρύγησαν ("were parched") in a wordplay; the Masoretic Text reads "like a hearth."
notes.101:9: Greek οἱ ἐπαινοῦντές με ("those who praised me") takes the underlying Hebrew root in the sense of "praise," whereas the Masoretic Text is usually understood as "those who deride/rage against me."
notes.101:21: Greek τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν τεθανατωμένων ("the sons of those put to death") literally translates a Hebrew idiom meaning those doomed to die.
notes.101:24: Greek ἀπεκρίθη ("He answered") differs from the Masoretic Text ("He weakened/afflicted"), introducing vv. 24-29 as direct speech to the Lord; the pronoun αὐτοῦ ("his") can also be read as referring to the Lord's strength ("His").
notes.101:26: The Septuagint includes Κύριε ("Lord") here and reads ἑλίξεις ("You will roll them up") in v. 27, the wording quoted in Hebrews 1:10-12.
notes.102:2: This Greek text reads αἰνέσεις ("praises"), whereas other Septuagint witnesses read ἀνταποδόσεις ("recompenses" or "benefits"), matching the Masoretic Text.
notes.102:5: Greek τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν σου ("your desire") renders a debated Hebrew word variously translated "your years," "your prime," or "your mouth."
notes.102:7: Greek τὰ θελήματα αὐτοῦ (plural, "His desires" or "His will") differs from the Masoretic Text, which reads "His deeds."
notes.102:14: Greek μνήσθητι is a second-person singular imperative ("Remember"), turning the clause into direct address to God, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "He remembers."
notes.102:16: In Greek, τὸν τόπον αὐτοῦ ("his place") is accusative, making the human being the subject ("he will no longer recognize his place"), whereas in the Masoretic Text "its place" is the subject ("its place knows it no more").
notes.103:1: The Greek text reads a doubled address ('Lord, Lord') with exclamatory 'how,' and uses exomologesis ('thanksgiving' or 'praise/confession') where the Hebrew text has 'splendor.'
notes.103:4: Greek angelous can mean 'angels' or 'messengers,' and pneumata can mean 'spirits' or 'winds' (the latter paralleling 'flaming fire').
notes.103:6: The Greek masculine genitive pronoun autou ('His') refers to God as wearer of the deep like a garment (echoing v. 2), unlike the Hebrew text's 'You covered it [the earth].'
notes.103:17: The Septuagint identifies the bird as a heron (erodios) and renders the clause with hegeitai auto ('leads it,' dative singular), differing markedly from the Hebrew wording about the stork's home in the fir trees.
notes.103:26: This Greek text lacks the clause about ships sailing there, uses drakon ('dragon') for the sea creature, and reads empaizein auto ('to play with' or 'to mock' it).
notes.104:4: The Greek reads the imperative verb κραταιώθητε ("be strengthened"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads a noun ("and His strength").
notes.104:22: The Greek reads τοῦ παιδεῦσαι ... ὡς ἑαυτόν ("to instruct ... as himself"), reflecting a different reading from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("to bind ... at his pleasure").
notes.104:27: The Greek uses the singular verb ἔθετο ("He placed"), making God the subject, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses a plural verb ("they performed").
notes.104:28: The Greek omits any negative particle ("and they rebelled against His words"), unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("and they did not rebel against His words").
notes.104:30: The Greek text here reads τῶν βασιλειῶν αὐτῶν ("of their kingdoms"), whereas other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew read "of their kings."
notes.105:7: Greek reads ἀναβαίνοντες ("as they went up"), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants than the Masoretic Text's "by the sea."
notes.105:15: Greek πλησμονήν means "fullness" or "satiety," in contrast to the Masoretic Text's "leanness" or "wasting disease."
notes.105:23: The Greek text here reads ἀπὸ θυμοῦ ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ("from the fury of His anger," echoing Exodus 32:12), whereas other Greek witnesses read τὴν ὀργὴν αὐτοῦ ("His wrath").
notes.105:32: Greek ὕδατος Ἀντιλογίας ("water of Contention," singular) translates the Hebrew place name Meribah ("waters of Meribah") rather than transliterating it.
notes.105:33: In context, τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ("his spirit") most naturally refers to Moses, though some interpret it as God's Spirit ("His Spirit"). Greek διέστειλεν literally means "spoke distinctly" or "pronounced," differing from the Masoretic Text's "spoke rashly."
notes.106:3: Greek θαλάσσης ("the sea") literally renders the Hebrew word for "sea" (often meaning "west") in the fourth compass position, where "south" might be expected.
notes.106:17: The Greek reads ἀντελάβετο αὐτῶν ("He helped them" or "came to their aid") rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "Fools."
notes.106:29: This critical Greek text reads the shorter clause καὶ ἔστησεν καταιγίδα αὐτῆς ("and He stilled its storm"), without the additional phrase "into a breeze" found in some Greek witnesses and the Hebrew.
notes.106:30: This critical Greek text reads ἐπιμελίᾳ θελήματος αὐτοῦ ("with the care of His will," an itacistic spelling of ἐπιμελείᾳ, "care"), whereas other Greek manuscripts read ἐπὶ λιμένα ("to a harbor") and/or plural "their."
notes.106:35: This critical Greek text reads λιμένας ("harbors," where other manuscripts read λίμνας, "pools") and omits the second clause ("and a waterless land into outlets of water") found in other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew.
notes.107:3: Greek ἐξεγερθήσομαι ὄρθρου means "I will awaken at dawn" (passive verb with genitive of time), in contrast to the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "I will awaken the dawn."
notes.107:8: The Septuagint reads "I will be exalted" (Ὑψωθήσομαι, vs. Hebrew "I will exult") and translates the place name Succoth literally as "the Valley of Tents" (τὴν κοιλάδα τῶν σκηνωμάτων).
notes.107:10: The Septuagint reads "basin of My hope" (λέβης τῆς ἐλπίδος μου, vs. Hebrew "washbasin"), uses the Greek geographical name Ἰδουμαία ("Idumea") for Hebrew Edom, and renders Hebrew "Philistines" with its standard term οἱ ἀλλόφυλοι ("the foreigners").
notes.107:14: Greek ἐξουδενώσει ("will bring to nothing" or "will treat with contempt") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "will tread down."
notes.108:1: "For the end" translates the standard Septuagint superscription phrase (Greek eis to telos). The Greek also makes "my praise" the direct object of "do not pass over in silence," rather than reading "God of my praise."
notes.108:6: Greek diabolos literally means "slanderer" or "accuser," matching the cognate verb "slander" in vv. 4, 20, and 29; elsewhere in biblical Greek the word also denotes the devil.
notes.108:20: The Greek text reads para Kyrio in the dative ("before the Lord"), whereas other witnesses and the Hebrew read "from the Lord" (referring to recompense from the Lord).
notes.108:23: The Greek text reads the third-person passive antanerethe ("was taken away"), referring to the declining shadow, rather than the variant first-person reading ("I was taken away").
notes.108:24: Greek di' elaion literally means "on account of oil," representing the Hebrew sense "for lack of oil."
notes.109:1: Greek uses kyrios twice ("the Lord said to my lord/Lord"); capitalizing "my Lord" and the pronouns in vv. 1-7 follows traditional messianic reading, as Greek manuscripts make no case distinction between a human royal lord and a divine Lord.
notes.109:3: The Septuagint differs markedly from the Hebrew here, reading "with You is dominion [Greek arche, also 'beginning'] ... from the womb before the morning star I brought You forth."
notes.109:5: Greek synethlasen ("shattered") is aorist indicative, contrasting with the future tenses in v. 6 and depicting the Lord's victory as already accomplished.
notes.109:6: Greek plerosei ptoma literally reads "He will fill [with] corpse/downfall" using a singular noun, taken either collectively ("fill them with corpses") or as "bring downfall to full measure."
notes.110:2: Greek exezetemena eis panta ta thelemata autou ("sought out for all His desires") reflects the Septuagint rendering, differing from the Hebrew sense "studied by all who delight in them."
notes.110:10: Greek auten ("it") is feminine singular, referring back to "wisdom" or "understanding," whereas the Hebrew has a plural pronoun referring to the commandments.
notes.111:3: Greek reads "Glory and wealth," whereas the Hebrew MT reads "Wealth and riches."
notes.111:4: The masculine singular adjectives "merciful and compassionate and righteous" have no explicit subject in Greek and may describe either the righteous man (continuing vv. 1-3, 5) or the Lord (cf. Ps 110:4).
notes.111:5: Greek literally reads "his words," reflecting the broad range of the underlying Hebrew term for "words" or "affairs."
notes.111:7: Greek reads "ready to hope," whereas the Hebrew MT reads "steadfast, trusting."
notes.112:1: Greek addresses "servants" (paides, also "children") without "of the Lord" and ends with "His name" rather than "the name of the Lord."
notes.112:3: Greek uses the present passive indicative "is praised" rather than a verbal adjective ("is to be praised").
notes.112:8: The pronoun in "His people" could alternatively refer to the needy man ("his people").
notes.112:9: The Greek participle "rejoicing" is genitive plural modifying "children," whereas the Hebrew MT and some Greek witnesses modify "mother" ("a joyful mother of children").
notes.113:2: Greek explicitly names "Judea" rather than "Judah," as in the Hebrew MT.
notes.113:6: This Greek text contains only the first clause ("Mountains, did you leap like rams?"), without the parallel line about the hills found in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.113:7: Greek uses a past indicative ("the earth was shaken"), whereas the Hebrew MT uses an imperative ("Tremble, earth").
notes.113:9: In the Septuagint, vv. 9-26 continue as part of Psalm 113 rather than starting a separate psalm (MT Ps 115); similarly, vv. 17-21 use past indicative verbs ("has hoped," "has blessed") where the Hebrew MT has imperatives and future verbs.
notes.113:25: Greek addresses the Lord in the second person ("praise You, Lord") and reads "into Hades" where the Hebrew MT reads "into silence"; v. 26 uses the hortatory subjunctive ("let us bless").
notes.114:1: The Greek text here reads 'God' (ho theos), whereas most Septuagint witnesses and the Hebrew MT (Ps 116:1) read 'the Lord.' Septuagint Psalms 114 and 115 together correspond to Hebrew Psalm 116.
notes.114:2: The Greek text reads 'in His days' (en tais hemerais autou) with the past-tense verb 'I called out,' whereas other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew MT read 'in my days' with a future verb ('I will call').
notes.114:5: The Greek text reads 'the Lord our God' (Kyrios ho theos hemon), where other Septuagint witnesses and the Hebrew MT read simply 'our God.' Both 'merciful' (eleemon) and 'shows mercy' (elea) derive from the same Greek root.
notes.114:6: Greek ta nepia literally means 'the infants' or 'little children,' reflecting the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew term for 'the simple.'
notes.114:9: Greek euaresteso ('I will be well-pleasing') follows a characteristic Septuagint idiom for the Hebrew phrase 'I will walk before the Lord'; similarly, verse 8 preserves the Septuagint third person ('He delivered') rather than the Hebrew second person ('You delivered').
notes.115:2: Greek ekstasis denotes being beside oneself in astonishment, bewilderment, or dismay, rendering the Hebrew term for 'alarm' or 'haste.' The Greek also uses the singular 'every person' (pas anthropos), echoed in Romans 3:4.
notes.115:3: The Greek text reads 'for what' (peri hon) without the word 'all' found in some other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew MT. The repeated verb antapodidomi ('repay' or 'give in return') reflects the Hebrew verb for dealing generously or recompensing.
notes.115:4: Verse 115:5 (corresponding to Hebrew Ps 116:14) is absent from this Greek textual tradition (Swete prints Codex Sinaiticus [א] here because Codex Vaticanus [B] is lacunose across Psalms 105:27-137:6, whereas the Sixtine/Brenton and Orthodox LXX editions include the longer wording repeating verse 9); the parallel vow statement appears in verse 9.
notes.115:7: Greek dierrhexas literally means 'You have torn apart' or 'broken,' a stronger verb than the Hebrew MT's 'loosed.'
notes.115:8: This Greek text preserves the shorter reading ending with 'a sacrifice of praise,' omitting the additional clause 'and I will call on the name of the Lord' found in the Hebrew MT (Ps 116:17) and some later Greek witnesses.
notes.116:1: Septuagint Psalm 116 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 117. Unlike the Hebrew second-person imperative, the Greek shifts to a third-person imperative ('let all the peoples praise Him') and uses the simple verb ainesatosan rather than the compound form quoted in Romans 15:11.
notes.116:2: Greek aletheia ('truth') and the explicit verb menei ('remains') reflect the Septuagint wording, where the Hebrew MT has 'faithfulness' without an explicit verb; Greek ekrataiothe ('has been made strong') renders the passive voice literally.
notes.117:2: The Greek text reads "house of Israel" (rather than simply "Israel" as in the Hebrew) and includes the clause "that He is good" in verses 2-4, matching the refrain of verse 1.
notes.117:5: Literally "answered me into a broad place" (or "heard me into a wide space"), a compressed Greek idiom meaning the Lord responded by bringing the psalmist out of distress (literally "pressure") into open space and relief.
notes.117:12: The Greek includes "a honeycomb" (kerion) and reads "they blazed up" (exekauthesan), whereas the Hebrew text describes the nations as bees that were extinguished like a fire of thorns.
notes.117:16: This Greek text contains only this single clause in verse 16, without repeating "the right hand of the Lord performed a mighty deed" as found in the Hebrew text and some Greek manuscripts.
notes.117:27: The Greek verb epephanen ("shone upon") can also mean "appeared to." In the second half, the Greek renders the command as arranging a festival with dense or leafy branches (en tois pykazousin) rather than binding a festal sacrifice with cords as in the Hebrew.
notes.118:38: The Greek text includes the preposition "εἰς" before "Your utterance" ("στῆσον τῷ δούλῳ σου εἰς τὸ λόγιόν σου"), creating an elliptical construction compared to witnesses that make "Your utterance" the direct object of "establish."
notes.118:47: Here and in 118:48, the Greek text has the second-person verb "ἠγάπησας" ("You loved"), rather than the first-person "I loved" found in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.118:50: The Greek text reads "οὐκ ἐξέκλινα" ("I have not turned aside from Your utterance"), rather than "Your utterance has given me life" as in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.118:75: The Greek text pairs "δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ" ("in righteousness and truth") in the dative and makes "Your judgments" the subject of the third-person plural verb "ἐταπείνωσάν με" ("have humbled me"), rather than the second-person "You humbled me."
notes.118:82: The Greek text ends with the declarative third-person plural "Παρεκάλεσάν με" ("They have comforted me"), rather than the question "When will You comfort me?" found in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.118:95: The Greek text contains only this clause ("τὰ δὲ μαρτύριά σου συνῆκα"), omitting the opening line about sinners waiting to destroy the psalmist found in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.118:102: The Greek text reads "κλιμάτων" ("regions" or "directions") rather than "κριμάτων" ("judgments"), an ancient variant differing by a single letter.
notes.118:114: The Greek text reads "τὸν λαόν σου" ("Your people") rather than "τὸν λόγον σου" ("Your word") as in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.118:147: The Greek text reads the third-person plural "προέφθασάν με" ("they came upon me") rather than the first-person "προέφθασα" ("I rose early"); in 118:148 it similarly reads "πρὸς σὲ ὀρθροῦν" ("rising early toward You") rather than "πρὸς ὄρθρον" ("before dawn").
notes.118:176: The Greek text reads "ζῆσον" ("give life to") rather than "ζήτησον" ("seek") found in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.119:1: Greek anabathmōn literally means "steps" or "stairs," the Septuagint rendering of the superscription traditionally known as "Songs of Ascents."
notes.119:3: The Greek uses the preposition pros ("against" or "in response to") with "a deceitful tongue," whereas the Hebrew treats the phrase as a vocative ("O deceitful tongue").
notes.119:4: Greek tois anthraxin tois erēmikois literally reads "the coals of the desert," rendering the Hebrew reference to coals of the broom tree (a desert shrub).
notes.119:5: Greek hē paroikia mou emakrynthē ("my sojourn has been prolonged") interprets the Hebrew consonants mšk verbally ("prolonged") rather than as the place name Meshech.
notes.119:7: The Greek adds dōrean ("without cause" or "for nothing"), a word not present in the Masoretic Hebrew text.
notes.120:3: Greek mē dōs is second-person singular ("Do not give"), contrasting with the third-person singular in Hebrew ("May He not let your foot slip").
notes.120:4: The Greek source text reads exypnōsei ("awaken" or "wake up"), a striking textual variant where most Greek witnesses read hypnōsei ("sleep," matching the Hebrew); taken literally, it implies that Israel's guardian never enters the cycle of drowsiness and waking.
notes.120:5: Greek skepē literally means "shelter" or "covering," where the Hebrew text reads "shade."
notes.120:7: The second verb is the aorist optative phylaxai ("may He guard," also formally identical to the infinitive "to guard") without a repeated subject, unlike witnesses that read the future indicative phylaxei ("will guard").
notes.120:8: The Greek reverses the Hebrew word order, reading "your coming in and your going out" (eisodon ... exodon) rather than "your going out and your coming in."
notes.121:3: Greek hēs hē metochē autēs epi to auto literally reads "whose fellowship (or participation) is together," contrasting with the Hebrew image of a city "bound firmly together."
notes.121:6: The Greek source text reverses the two clauses found in most Greek witnesses and the Hebrew text, placing "and prosperity for those who love you" first and using the dative tē Ierousalēm ("for Jerusalem").
notes.121:7: The Greek source text reads "your peace" (adding "your"), renders Hebrew "rampart/wall" as dynamei ("strength"), and uses the rare compound pyrgobaresin ("fortified towers" or "citadels").
notes.121:8: The punctuation and the conjunction de ("And," where other witnesses read dē, "indeed") attach "for the sake of my brothers and my neighbors" to the blessing of verse 7 rather than to "I was speaking peace concerning you."
notes.121:9: The Greek source text reads simply exezētēsa soi ("I sought on your behalf"), omitting the direct object agatha ("good things") found in other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew text.
notes.122:1: Greek anabathmōn literally means "of the steps," the Septuagint title corresponding to the Songs of Ascents; Greek also reads singular "in heaven" (en tō ouranō) with "who dwells" (katoikounta).
notes.122:2: Greek has plural "hands" (cheiras) in both comparisons, uses the Septuagintal infinitive construction heōs hou oikteirēsai hēmas ("until He has compassion on us"), and distinguishes "have compassion" (oikteireō) here from "have mercy" (eleeō) in v. 3.
notes.122:4: Greek uses nominatives with datives ("reproach to those who prosper, and contempt to the proud"), which can be read either as an imprecation against the arrogant or as a literalistic rendering of the Hebrew idiom for scorn coming from them. In vv. 3-4, "filled" renders passive plēthynō ("be multiplied / filled abundantly").
notes.123:1: Greek en hēmin literally means "among us" (or "in us"), distinct from the Hebrew idiom "for us / on our side."
notes.123:4: In vv. 4-5, Greek makes "our soul" the grammatical subject ("our soul would have passed through") rather than the waters sweeping over the soul, and uses singular "the water" (to hydōr). The aorist indicatives continue the contrary-to-fact apodosis introduced with an in v. 3.
notes.123:5: Greek anypostaton literally means "not to be withstood" or "offering no footing," hence "overwhelming."
notes.123:7: Greek uses the passive of rhyomai ("was rescued ... were rescued") where the Hebrew reads "escaped," and pairs "hunters" (thēreuontōn) with "prey" (thēran) in v. 6.
notes.124:1: Greek construes "Jerusalem" (Ierousalēm) as the object of the participle "the one who dwells" (ho katoikōn) at the end of v. 1, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text opens v. 2 with "Jerusalem." "Will never be shaken" translates the idiomatic ou saleuthēsetai eis ton aiōna.
notes.124:3: Greek uses the transitive future active aphēsei ("He will not leave," with the Lord as implied subject) and plural "of the sinners" (tōn hamartōlōn), rather than the Hebrew "the scepter of wickedness shall not rest."
notes.124:5: Greek strangalias literally denotes twisted knots, entanglements, or crooked ways, with no possessive pronoun ("their").
notes.125:1: The Greek superscription "of the steps" (τῶν ἀναβαθμῶν) corresponds to the Hebrew title commonly translated "of ascents." "Those who have been comforted" (παρακεκλημένοι) faithfully renders the Septuagint reading, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "those who dream."
notes.125:2: The future tense "they will say" (ἐροῦσιν) follows the Greek verbatim, and "did great things with them" renders the Greek idiom ἐμεγάλυνεν τοῦ ποιῆσαι μετ᾽ αὐτῶν (lit., "magnified to do with them").
notes.125:4: The Greek uses the singular "winter torrent" (ὁ χειμάρρους, a seasonal wadi) and "in the south" (ἐν τῷ νότῳ), corresponding to the Hebrew plural streams in the Negev.
notes.126:2: Following the Septuagint closely, the Greek reads "to get up after sitting down" (rather than staying up late) and introduces the final clause with temporal "when" (ὅταν) rather than "for so."
notes.126:3: In this Greek text, "the reward of the fruit of her womb" places "fruit" in the genitive (τοῦ καρποῦ) and includes "her" (αὐτῆς), placing the phrase in apposition to "sons" as the Lord's inheritance.
notes.126:4: "Those who have been shaken out" (τῶν ἐκτετιναγμένων) reflects the Septuagint reading the underlying Hebrew term from the root meaning "shake out" rather than "youth."
notes.126:5: The Septuagint reads "his desire" (τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν αὐτοῦ) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "his quiver," and this Greek text shifts from singular "he will not be put to shame" (καταισχυνθήσεται) to plural "when they speak to their enemies."
notes.127:2: The Greek reads the plural "the fruits of your labors" (τοὺς καρποὺς τῶν πόνων σου), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the labor of your hands."
notes.127:3: The Greek participle εὐθηνοῦσα means "flourishing" or "thriving," and ἐν τοῖς κλίτεσι literally means "on the sides" of the house.
notes.128:3: Greek "etektainon" literally means "were building" or "worked as craftsmen" (contrasting with the Hebrew "plowed"), and "ten anomian auton" means "their lawlessness" (contrasting with the Hebrew "their furrows").
notes.128:4: The Greek reads "auchena" ("neck," singular), where the Hebrew text reads "cords."
notes.128:8: The Greek text here reads "eph' hemas" ("upon us") and the future "eulogesomen" ("we will bless"), where other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew read "upon you" and "we bless" or "we have blessed."
notes.129:4: Greek "ho hilasmos" means "propitiation" or "atonement" (rendering the Hebrew "forgiveness"). The Septuagint also reads "For the sake of Your name" (joining it to verse 5), where the Hebrew reads "so that You may be feared."
notes.129:5: The Greek reads "eis ton nomon autou" ("for His law"), contrasting with the Hebrew "in His word." This Greek text also has no explicit direct object ("for You") after "hypemeina" ("I waited").
notes.129:6: The Greek reads "from the morning watch until night" (contrasting with the Hebrew "more than watchmen for the morning"). This Greek witness also omits the exhortation "let Israel hope in the Lord" present in other manuscripts and the Hebrew of verse 7.
notes.130:2: This Greek text connects "ei me etapeinophronoun" ("but rather I was humble-minded") to verse 1, then reads "kai hypsosa" ("and I lifted up") and "heos antapodoseis" ("until You repay"). Other Greek manuscripts read "alla" ("but") and "hos" ("so") as an oath, while the Hebrew reads "I have calmed and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with its mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me."
notes.131:3: Literally "If I will enter..." (and similarly in v. 4), a Hebraistic oath formula expressing an emphatic negative; verse 4 also includes the Greek phrase "or rest to my temples," absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.131:7: The Greek text shifts from first-person singular "I will enter" (εἰσελεύσομαι) to plural "we will worship" (προσκυνήσομεν); likewise, verse 9 reads aorist "clothed themselves" (ἐνεδύσαντο) alongside future "will exult."
notes.131:15: Translating the Greek text "her widow" (τὴν χήραν αὐτῆς), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "her provision."
notes.131:17: The Greek text reads "for your anointed one" (τῷ χριστῷ σου), apparently addressing Zion or reflecting a variant influenced by verse 10, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other witnesses read "for my anointed one."
notes.131:18: Greek ἁγίασμα ("holiness," also in v. 8) can also mean "sanctuary" or "consecration," corresponding here to the Hebrew term for a royal crown or sign of consecration.
notes.132:1: Unlike the exclamation in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("How good and how pleasant..."), the Greek frames the verse as a rhetorical question ("what is good or what is pleasant, except...").
notes.132:2: Greek ᾤα denotes the border, edge, or hem of a garment (singular ἐνδύματος), corresponding to the Hebrew phrase often rendered "collar of his robes."
notes.133:1: The Greek text reads "who stand in the courts of the house of our God," without "in the house of the Lord" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses, and places "in the nights" at the beginning of verse 2.
notes.133:2: Literally "toward the holy things" (εἰς τὰ ἅγια), the standard Greek designation for the sanctuary or holy place.
notes.133:3: The Greek uses the future indicative εὐλογήσει ("will bless") rather than an optative wish ("may... bless").
notes.134:1: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("servants of the Lord"), the Greek places "the Lord" in the accusative as the direct object of "praise" and leaves "servants" as a vocative.
notes.134:12: The Greek reads "Israel His servant" (matching 135:22), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Israel his people."
notes.134:14: Our Greek text reads "has compassion on" (oikteirei) rather than "will judge" (krinei, as in other Septuagint witnesses and the Hebrew). The passive "will be comforted" (paraklethesetai) is a Septuagint idiom conveying relenting or being moved to pity.
notes.134:21: The Greek psalm ends without a concluding "Hallelujah," which instead stands at the opening of Psalm 135 (MT 136).
notes.135:6: The Greek verb "established" (stereosanti, lit. "made firm") and singular "the water" (to hydor) reflect the Septuagint text rather than the Hebrew "spread out ... the waters."
notes.135:7: The Greek adds "alone" (mono), echoing verse 4; the word is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.135:12: The Greek reads "with an uplifted arm" (en brachioni hypselo, lit. "a high arm") where the Hebrew has "an outstretched arm."
notes.135:26: Our Greek text reads "the Lord of heaven" (to kyrio tou ouranou), whereas other Septuagint witnesses and the Hebrew read "the God of heaven."
notes.136:1: The Septuagint includes the superscription "For David" (To Dauid), which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (MT Psalm 137).
notes.136:2: The Greek "our musical instruments" (ta organa hemon) is broader than the Hebrew "our lyres."
notes.136:3: The Greek refers to "those who led us away" (rather than "our tormentors") and omits a word for "mirth" or "hymn" before the quotation, with "said" supplied for the elliptical syntax.
notes.136:5: Unlike the active Hebrew verb ("forget [its skill]"), the Greek uses the passive optative "be forgotten" (epilestheie).
notes.136:8: The Greek reads "you wretched one" (he talaiporos) rather than "doomed to be destroyed," and repeats the same root three times ("repay ... repayment ... repaid").
notes.137:1: The Greek text includes the clause "because You heard the words of my mouth" and renders the Hebrew term for heavenly beings or gods as "angels" (angelon).
notes.137:2: The Greek phrase epi pan onoma to hagion sou is syntactically ambiguous and may be construed either as "Your holy name above everything" (followed here) or as "Your holy one/sanctuary above every name."
notes.137:7: The Greek text literally reads "against the wrath of enemies You stretched out my hands" (echthron ... cheiras mou), whereas other manuscripts read "my enemies" and "Your hand."
notes.138:9: The Greek text reads kat' orthon ("straight ahead" or "in a straight course"), whereas other manuscripts read kat' orthron ("at dawn").
notes.138:12: The Greek text preserves a shorter reading here, omitting the clauses found in other witnesses ("for darkness will not be darkened from You, and night will be illuminated as day"); the feminine pronoun "its" (autes) refers back to "night" in verse 11.
notes.138:14: The Greek verb ethaumastothes is second person singular, addressing God ("You have been shown fearfully wondrous"), rather than first person singular as in the Hebrew text.
notes.138:16: The Greek text reads to akatergaston sou eidosan hoi ophthalmoi mou ("My eyes saw Your unfinished work"), reversing the pronouns found in most other witnesses; hemeras may be understood as temporal genitive ("by day") or accusative plural ("for days").
notes.138:20: This difficult Septuagint verse reads ereis eis dialogismon ("You will speak concerning a thought") and tas poleis sou ("Your cities"), reflecting a different parsing of the Hebrew consonants.
notes.138:24: The Greek text reads ei ides anomias ("if You have seen lawless deeds"), where other manuscripts read ei hodos anomias ("if there is a way of lawlessness").
notes.139:4: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, a musical or liturgical pause marker corresponding to Hebrew Selah (also in verses 6 and 9).
notes.139:9: The Greek literally reads "away from my desire" (apo tes epithymias mou), reflecting a different division and reading of the Hebrew than "the desires of the wicked."
notes.139:11: The Greek text reads "coals of fire ... on the earth, and You will cast them down," whereas other Septuagint witnesses read "coals; into fire You will cast them down."
notes.139:12: The Greek text here is shorter than other witnesses, omitting an opening clause concerning a talkative or slanderous man not being established on the earth.
notes.140:3: Greek "thyran perioches" literally means "a door of enclosure" (or "fortification"), an LXX phrase for a protective barrier restraining speech.
notes.140:4: Greek "syndoiaso" (from "syndoiazo", a spelling variant of "syndyazo", "join" or "associate with") and "ton eklekton auton" ("their chosen ones", or neuter "their choice things") reflect an LXX reading distinct from the Hebrew MT ("eat of their delicacies").
notes.140:5: The LXX reads "in their pleasures" (Greek "eudokiais", good pleasures or delights) rather than the Hebrew MT "against their evil deeds," and the doubled adverb "eti kai eti" emphasizes persistence ("yet again and again").
notes.140:6: This Greek text reads "hoi krataioi auton" ("their strong ones") and "edynethesan" ("they prevailed", from "dynamai"), whereas other LXX witnesses read "their judges" and "hedynthesan" ("they were sweet").
notes.140:10: Greek "autou" ("his") is singular, either used distributively for each sinner's own net or referring to the Lord's net; "kata monas" ("alone") is an LXX reading differing from the Hebrew MT.
notes.141:1: Greek "Syneseos" ("Of understanding") renders the Hebrew heading "maskil," and the dative "to Dauid" is literally "for David."
notes.141:5: Unlike the Hebrew MT imperatives ("Look... and see"), the LXX uses first-person imperfect verbs describing David's own searching, and this Greek witness reads "hoti" ("for/that") rather than "kai" ("and").
notes.141:8: The Greek text includes the vocative "Kyrie" ("Lord") and reads "hypomenousin" ("will wait for"), where the Hebrew MT reads "will surround."
notes.142:1: The historical clause "when his son pursues him" (referring to Absalom) is an LXX superscription absent from the Hebrew MT, using the historical present verb "katadiokei."
notes.142:3: This Greek text omits the opening clause ("For the enemy has pursued my soul") found in other witnesses, leaving the adversary as the implicit subject of "He"; Greek "nekrous aionos" literally means "dead ones of an age" (those long dead, or dead forever).
notes.142:6: "Interlude" translates Greek "diapsalma," the LXX rendering of the Hebrew liturgical or musical term "selah."
notes.142:10: This Greek text reads "Your Holy Spirit" ("to hagion") rather than "Your good Spirit" ("to agathon") as in other LXX and Hebrew witnesses, and "en te eutheia" ("in the straight way") lacks the noun "land" ("ge").
notes.142:11: In verses 11-12 the LXX uses future indicative verbs ("You will...") rather than imperatives, and the Greek punctuation links "in Your righteousness" with the preceding clause "You will keep me alive."
notes.143:1: The Septuagint superscription uniquely adds "against Goliath" (or "concerning Goliath", Greek πρὸς τὸν Γολιάδ), linking the psalm to David's contest with Goliath, and reads "my God" where the Masoretic Text has "my rock".
notes.143:3: The Greek passive verb ἐγνώσθης ("You were made known to him") differs from the active reading of the Masoretic Text ("that You take knowledge of him").
notes.143:10: Following the Greek punctuation, "From an evil sword" begins the plea completed by "deliver me" in 143:11, rather than modifying "redeems David His servant" as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.143:12: Throughout verses 12-14 the Septuagint uses third-person pronouns ("whose sons... their daughters..."), describing the material prosperity of the foreigners rather than praying for "our" sons as in the Masoretic Text; it also reads "temple" (ναοῦ) rather than "palace".
notes.143:15: The Greek begins with a finite verb, ἐμακάρισαν ("They called blessed"), where the Hebrew reads "Blessed is the people."
notes.144:6: The Greek text shifts from third-person plural ("they will tell") to first-person singular ("I will recount it") and includes a third clause ("and they will speak of Your might") attested in major Septuagint witnesses.
notes.144:9: The Greek text reads τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν ("to those who endure" or "to those who wait patiently"), whereas the Masoretic Text and some Septuagint manuscripts read "to all".
notes.144:13: The second sentence ("Faithful is the Lord in His words, and holy in all His works") preserves the nun line of this acrostic psalm, present in the Septuagint, Dead Sea Scrolls, and Syriac though absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.144:16: The Greek uses the plural "Your hands" where the Masoretic Text has the singular, and the genitive εὐδοκίας ("goodwill," "favor," or "good pleasure") expresses what every living creature is filled with.
notes.145:1: The Septuagint superscription uniquely attributes this psalm to the post-exilic prophets Haggai and Zechariah.
notes.145:4: The Greek shifts from singular pronouns ("His spirit... his earth") in the first half of the verse to plural ("all their thoughts") in the second half.
notes.145:8: The Greek reverses the order of the first two clauses relative to the Masoretic Text and reads σοφοῖ ("makes wise") rather than "opens the eyes of" the blind.
notes.145:9: The Greek term προσήλυτος ("proselyte") renders the Hebrew word for resident alien or newcomer and in Hellenistic Jewish usage also denotes a Gentile convert living under God's care.
notes.146:1: In the Septuagint, Psalms 146 and 147 divide Hebrew Psalm 147 into two psalms (MT 147:1-11 and 147:12-20), and Psalms 146-148 share the superscription attributing them to Haggai and Zechariah. The Greek reads 'for a psalm is good' rather than the Hebrew 'for it is good to sing praises to our God.'
notes.146:4: The Greek reads 'multitudes of stars' (πλήθη ἄστρων) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'the number of the stars.'
notes.146:7: The Greek imperative ἐξάρξατε literally means 'begin' or 'lead off' in song or musical performance.
notes.146:8: The clause 'and green vegetation for the service of people' is present in the Septuagint (paralleling Psalm 103:14 LXX / 104:14 MT) but absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.147:3: Literally 'the fat of wheat' (στέαρ πυροῦ), a biblical idiom referring to the richest, choicest portion of the wheat.
notes.147:5: Here and in verse 6 the Greek uses genitive participles dependent on 'of Him' (αὐτοῦ) at the end of verse 4. The Greek also reads 'mist' (ὁμίχλην) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'frost.'
notes.147:7: Unlike the Hebrew causative ('He causes His wind to blow'), the Greek uses the intransitive verb πνεύσει with 'His wind' (τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ) as its subject.
notes.147:9: The Greek has an active third-person singular verb with God as subject ('He did not reveal His judgments to them') where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'they have not known them,' and lacks the closing 'Hallelujah' of MT 147:20.
notes.148:3: The Greek coordinates 'and the light' (καὶ τὸ φῶς) as a separate element rather than the Hebrew construct phrase 'all stars of light' (shining stars).
notes.148:5: The clause 'He Himself spoke and they came into being' (αὐτὸς εἶπεν καὶ ἐγενήθησαν) appears in the Septuagint (echoing Psalm 32:9 LXX / 33:9 MT) but is not in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.148:8: The Greek reads 'ice' (κρύσταλλος) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'smoke' or 'vapor.'
notes.148:13: Literally 'His thanksgiving' or 'His acknowledgment' (ἡ ἐξομολόγησις αὐτοῦ), taken as an objective genitive ('thanksgiving to Him'); the Septuagint links the underlying Hebrew word for 'majesty/splendor' to the root meaning 'give thanks.'
notes.148:14: The Greek text translated here moves directly from 'the horn of His people' to 'for the sons of Israel, a people drawing near to Him,' without the phrase 'praise for all His godly ones' or the closing 'Hallelujah' found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other witnesses.
notes.149:4: The Septuagint reads 'will exalt' (Greek hypsosei), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'will adorn' or 'will beautify.'
notes.149:6: Greek 'throats' is literally singular ('in their throat'), used distributively; 'exaltations' echoes the verb 'will exalt' in verse 4.
notes.149:9: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Greek text has no closing 'Hallelujah' at the end of Psalm 149, placing it instead at the beginning of Psalm 150.
notes.150:1: Greek en tois hagiois autou is plural and ambiguous in gender, meaning either 'in His holy places' or 'in His sanctuary' (neuter, matching the spatial parallel) or 'among His holy ones' (masculine).
notes.150:4: Greek organon is a general word for a musical instrument (as in 136:2 and 151:2); the Hebrew here names a pipe or flute.
notes.150:6: Greek pasa pnoe literally means 'every breath,' used as a poetic figure for every breathing creature.
notes.151:1: Psalm 151 stands in the Septuagint outside the 150-psalm collection; Greek idiographos eis Dauid literally means 'written in his own hand, pertaining to David.'
notes.151:4: Or 'His angel'; Greek angelos can mean either a human messenger (here referring to the prophet Samuel, who anointed David in 1 Samuel 16) or a heavenly angel.
notes.151:6: Greek allophylos literally means 'foreigner' or 'one of another tribe' and is the Septuagint's regular designation for a Philistine.
notes.151:7: Greek ten par autou machairan literally means 'the sword from him,' referring to Goliath's own sword taken from his side.
